text:
Best from the hip review of the top personal agents I’ve seen. 

I’ve been testing a bunch and what Riley concludes with is basically what I’ve discovered as well: they are all being updated so rapidly that by the time you test one, another has ten more features, ultimately making them converge. 

Dots has been my workhorse given my heavy use of Codex, and I think that’s the best way to approach these agents - pick the ecosystem you’re most exposed to and use that agent. 

Dots with local computer use is goated.
author: rileybrown
quoted_text:
My unfiltered thoughts on personal agents.

Grokbot has the best UI and it’s arguably the best overall. In a lot of ways they’re ahead. Their desktop app feels the best, and their multi-bot coordination is great: you can set a team lead and it passes tasks to the other bots. Grokbot also has the best “webhook” feature, which means you can easily turn outside events into triggers that start your agents. That speeds up background workflows like watching your email, Slack and more. It also has Cursor integration, so for bigger tasks Grokbot can spin up a Cursor cloud session with any model (until OpenAI cuts SpaceX off from their models, which I think will happen soon). Unfortunately, running frontier models through Cursor costs more than Claude or Codex. Still, they’re the only ones embracing a team of agents. It’s a really cool idea, but the more bots you have, the more time you spend managing and maintaining them. I’m starting to think one bot with different threads/channels is the right answer, which I’ll get to with Claude Duet.

dots by OpenAI is rough around the edges right now, but it’s probably the most powerful if you use Codex, which I do. dots can spin up Codex sessions in the cloud or locally on your computer. So if you have coding or video editing workflows that need your local files, this is very useful. Codex computer use is also the best in the world: your dot can spin up a local Codex session that fully controls your computer, as long as it’s on. Their real-time voice is incredible. If you have your email and work tools connected, try this: go on a walk with headphones in, ask the agent to summarize your emails, have it draft replies and read them back to you, then send them off. If I remember right, this is close to a workflow you (Tim) used to have with your VAs before AI. It’s my favorite use case for personal agents. The one downside is that you have to call your agent, and it’s an awful experience. It literally rings, and it’s annoying.

Muse by Meta is a toy. I’ve talked to a bunch of finance people I play poker with who all tried it and set up automations, and they all said it doesn’t reliably do what they want. It’s fast, and its user numbers will probably keep growing. But it’s basically free: you get a TON of usage without paying a dime. That’s NOT a trade I’m willing to make. An agent doing high-leverage tasks should be running at the Opus 5.5 or GPT 6.1 Sol level.

Claude Duet - is in early access, so unfortunately not everyone can use it yet. First things first, it runs on Opus 5.5, the best model in the world. I’ve only had access for 72 hours, but Duet feels different from the others. It’s not a personified agent like Grokbot, dot or Muse, which gives it a more professional vibe that I like. When you ask your Duet agent to do something, it spins up a task, which is a new chat thread. All your threads show up in a Tasks tab, so it’s easy to see everything Duet is working on or has finished. And instead of creating more agents (like Grokbot), you create channels, just like Slack (I can tell @anthropic is Slack-pilled). I have a content channel, a finances channel, etc., which keeps different kinds of tasks separate. The only other app I’ve seen do this is Buzz by @jack, and it’s a good experience. Their strong point is documents (artifacts). If you want decks, high-quality docs or design mockups, Opus just wins. Period. It’s not close right now. Their weak point is real-time voice. It’s the worst of the bunch and borderline unusable, though I think they only added it a few days ago.

Instinct lives in iMessage, has no app, and doesn’t do anything notable besides show you product suggestions you didn’t ask for. (Not ads, according to their team.)

My hot take: 
The VM is overrated. SpaceX, OpenAI and Meta all talk about the VM your agent can use and feature it in their marketing. It’s not as useful as you’d think, because more and more websites block bots that visit their site on the cloud VM. All of these companies promise their agents can make payments, but most payments either take forever or get blocked altogether. SpaceX has a cool workaround with Grokbot that routes traffic through your computer so it uses your IP address. But I’d much rather the agent just USE my computer for the task, like dot does by handing it off to Codex. Also, i don't think normal people care about the virtual computer. If anything they get offended they have to "stream a computer". 

The problem with personal agents: by the time you read this, pick one, and test it for 7 days, every one of them will have released 10 new features and the whole landscape will have changed. It’s nearly impossible to keep up.

text:
1 Corinthians 6 is so profound. 💯 We will judge the angels?!

Paul rebukes the Corinthians for taking disputes with fellow Christians to secular (pagan) courts instead of resolving them within the church. He points out that believers will one day judge the world and even angels, so they should be capable of handling ordinary matters among themselves. Going to outside courts is already a defeat; it would be better to be wronged or cheated than to wrong or cheat a brother. 

He then lists behaviors that exclude people from the kingdom of God (sexual immorality, idolatry, adultery, theft, greed, drunkenness, and others) and reminds the Corinthians that some of them once lived that way. They have been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God

Paul responds to the Corinthian slogan “All things are lawful for me.” He agrees in principle but adds that not everything is beneficial and that believers should not be mastered by anything. The body is not meant for sexual immorality but for the Lord (who will raise it), and the Lord is for the body.
Believers’ bodies are members of Christ; therefore they must not be joined to a prostitute (which creates a “one flesh” union). Sexual immorality is uniquely a sin against one’s own body. The body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, who dwells in believers. They do not belong to themselves—they were bought at a price. The chapter ends with the command to glorify God in your body.

Core message: Because believers belong to Christ and will share in his future judgment, they should handle community disputes with wisdom and restraint, and they should treat their bodies as sacred—honoring God rather than using them for sexual immorality.

One of the world's largest banks has officially entered the retail stablecoin market, bringing digital currencies to millions of existing customers.

HSBC has launched RedCoin (RCHKD), its first Hong Kong dollar-backed stablecoin, through its popular PayMe payment application. HSBC is introducing stablecoin functionality into an existing ecosystem with:

• More than 3.3 MILLION users.
• Over 100,000 supported merchants.
• Instant peer-to-peer transfers and merchant payments.
• A regulated stablecoin redeemable 1:1 for Hong Kong dollars.

Eligible PayMe users will be able to activate their stablecoin wallets directly within the app as the rollout expands over the coming days.

The bank also plans to integrate RedCoin into its Hong Kong mobile banking app later this year, allowing customers to use the stablecoin to subscribe to tokenized investment products, including an upcoming share class of its HKD money market fund.

Future expansion into corporate and institutional payments is also planned.

$GRIFT 正进入一个有趣的阶段，市场参与者开始关注其价格走势的变化，以及后续动向背后可能蕴含的信号。

在模因币（meme coin）市场中，初期的上涨仅仅是整体局势的一部分。价格剧烈波动后的表现，往往能揭示出关于市场情绪、买方信心以及持仓者是否愿意继续持有头寸的重要线索。@Griftwrld

对于 GRIFT 而言，关键在于它能否在经历近期的上涨势头后，建立起一个稳定的交易区间。

盘整阶段往往反映了市场动态的转变：部分交易者会选择获利了结，而另一些交易者则在寻找入场机会。

如果价格在保持稳定的同时，买盘兴趣重新回升，市场参与者可能会开始留意是否会出现新一轮的行情启动。然而，如果波动持续，或者价格跌破了关键支撑位，那么整体市场前景可能会随之改变。

0x9f4BA41F91a59A34e17eE8C9EB3A51363B11aBD5

交易量同样值得密切关注。在盘整期间，如果交易活跃度保持稳定，可能意味着市场兴趣依然存在；反之，若交易量萎缩，则可能表明市场参与度正在下降。流动性、买盘压力以及抛售活动，都将是判断市场后续走向的重要考量因素。

quoted_text:
$GRIFT 的价格结构值得关注；其近期的走势表明，这不仅仅是一次简单的短期上涨。@Griftwrld

CA：0x9f4BA41F91a59A34e17eE8C9EB3A51363B11aBD5

在瞬息万变的表情包市场中，价格的突然飙升固然能吸引眼球，但之后发生的事情往往更有意思。对于小市值代币而言，在强劲上涨后能否维持相对稳定的交易区间，是一个值得密切关注的信号。GRIFT 并未将此前的涨幅悉数回吐，而是似乎进入了一个市场参与者正在评估其后续方向的阶段。

这种从快速增长向盘整阶段的过渡值得深究。在初期行情吸引交易者入场后，市场往往会进入调整期，买卖双方在此期间建立新的平衡。如果价格能够持续稳固在既定区间内，这种结构或许能为后续再次尝试上攻奠定基础。当然，最终走势如何，仍需观察后续的价格表现，而非仅仅依赖当前的盘整形态。

另一个值得关注的因素是交易活跃度。若在价格结构保持相对稳定的同时，成交量依然维持在一定水平，则可能意味着市场兴趣仍在持续——当然，评估成交量时，还需结合流动性、波动率以及买卖压力的分布情况综合考量。对于 GRIFT 而言，观察市场参与度是否保持稳定，有助于更清晰地判断当前市场的信心与共识。

这一阶段最耐人寻味之处在于，下一波重大行情或许就孕育在当前的盘整期内。

若后续出现伴随成交量放大的有效突破，可能会再次引发市场关注；反之，如果价格跌破既定区间，则意味着当前的结构正在走弱。在明确的方向出现之前，保持耐心并进行细致观察至关重要。

ALERT! Our system detected a suspicious transaction targeting @x100global on Ethereum, resulting in an estimated loss of $4.75M. The root cause stems from a governance design flaw that allowed the attacker to acquire two of three Senate seats using flash-loan-funded X tokens and immediately approve and execute a malicious treasury proposal within the same transaction.

The attacker purchased X tokens using flash-loaned funds, distributed them to two controlled contracts, and froze them in the Freezer to obtain Senate seats. The attacker then created and supplied liquidity to a PancakeSwap V3 X-USDT pool. Using the captured majority, the attacker executed a proposal directing the Freezer to swap 400,000 X tokens into that pool with the minimum output set to zero, receiving only about 35.68 USDT. Finally, the attacker withdrew the liquidity, sold part of the recovered X tokens through the existing Uniswap V3 X-USDT pool, and repaid the flash loan.

text:
It’s true and overwhelmingly positive that blockchains are being adopted through tokenized RWAs and fiat stablecoins. I understand the push to rebrand the industry around Finance (or grouping it with other Frontier tech) rather than "crypto".

But to me, the word crypto has always encapsulated core beliefs around cypherpunk tech, decentralization, and the creation of entirely new economic institutions.

I believe "crypto" in its original sense will make a resurgence in the years ahead. As public blockchain rails become deeply integrated into legacy system, they’ll also lay the foundation for something far more transformative: the dominance of decentralized exchange, the proliferation of futarchy, the global preference toward non-sovereign money, and entirely new forms of economic coordination.

We’ll need a word to distinguish these new institutions from the traditional ones they’re replacing.

Fortunately, we already have one.

So yeah, I’m going to keep calling it crypto.

text:
十年前，当 DeepMind 还在庆祝 AI 学会打雅达利游戏时，Demis Hassabis 就跟员工说：有一天，我们会靠这项技术拿诺贝尔奖。

2024 年，他真的拿到了。

《华尔街日报》刚刚发表了一篇关于 Hassabis 的人物特写，我觉得这个人的经历简直像一本提前写好结局的科幻小说。

4 岁开始下国际象棋，小到要坐在电话簿上才能看见棋盘；12 岁跻身世界顶尖的同龄棋手；16 岁进入游戏公司研究 AI；2010 年创办 DeepMind，后来接连做出了 AlphaGo 和 AlphaFold，后者预测了超过 2 亿个蛋白质结构，最终让他获得诺贝尔化学奖。

但他觉得自己真正想做的事情才刚刚开始。

Hassabis 对人生的规划只有两步：

Step 1：Solve intelligence.

Step 2：Solve everything else.

他最近甚至把 AGI 到来的预期从 3～5 年缩短到了 2～3 年。他给 AGI 设计的终极考题也很有意思，只让 AI 学习 1901 年以前的人类知识，看看它能不能独立发现爱因斯坦在 1905 年提出的那些物理学突破。

我一直觉得 Hassabis 是当下 AI 行业里特别值得研究的人。大多数公司还在为模型排名、用户增长和商业收入打得不可开交，他已经开始考虑如何用 AGI 重新发明药物研发，甚至破解物理学的终极难题。

在采访的最后，记者问他，假如有一天真的解决了智能问题，他最想做什么？

他的回答是，和 AGI 以及人类科学家一起，继续研究现实世界的本质，寻找下一层物理学规律。

对于一个已经用 AI 拿过诺贝尔奖的人来说，这种野心很难被简单归类为吹牛。

当然，解决智能距离解决一切还有很长的路。但至少 Hassabis 已经证明过一次，看起来像科幻小说的目标，确实可能成为现实。

本次RH链@RobinhoodCrypto 上，已经让大多数人体感非常不好，正从繁荣向深渊跌落，那么，能止住吗？接下来会发生什么？可以复盘一下前两轮周期，预判一下接下来会如何发展：

2020年，defi-summer时期，defi挖矿——开启新一轮代币分发模式，当时也处于牛初时期，第一波爆发后，龙头UNI从最高9.5U回调到1.8U，跌幅约80%，回调盘整三个月后，开启第二轮疯涨，从1.8U涨到45U，涨了25倍。当时很多币都回调90%以上后，再上涨大几十倍（如sushi，YFI，cake等）。

2023年，铭文时期，打铭文——又开启另一种新的代币分发模式，去VC公平分发，也是处于牛初时期，第一波爆发后，龙头 ORDI从29U跌到3U，跌幅近90%，回调盘整约5个月，全网都在说“铭文已死”，最后用了三个月，拉了30倍，到95U。当时也诞生了几百倍的神盘 SATS

2026年，股票/meme组pair，公平lauchpad，结合v4 hooks——或许将开启又一种新的代币分发模式，defi 2.0 summer时代可期，目前也是牛市初期：

首先，股票代表传统资产，meme代表币圈资产，两者合二为一，股票/meme组pair，捆绑叙事，非常合理

其次，代币发射后，代币交易税收入的分发模式，即解决了传统VC那种defi 挖矿的增发抛售隐患，又解决了完全公平发射导致的前期无收入无激励冷启动难的问题。交易税收入合理分配给项目方，创作者，交易者，以及发射台等，各方都有可以得到激励，PVE

再次，v4 hooks的出现，为新币发射毕业后，交易税收益可延续至整个代币生命周期，整套交易税激励模型可以一直持续。hooks的合约开放，还可以将整个代币分发变得更加灵活。所以hooks是一个非常关键的不可或缺的创新和基建

最后，对于发射的新项目（不一定只是meme)来说，以上的发币模式即解决了新项目冷启动的激励问题，又解决了代币是全流通，不会导致因代币增发而抛售的隐患。另外，优质的新项目后期自身也能创造收益。这种新币交易税收益+新项目本身创造的收益，可以为整个项目增加更多收益，=更多的回购销毁，=更多资金来发展项目，=币价螺旋上涨

Defi 2.0配合新的代币分发模式，这种PVE模式是可持续的，接下来需要的是：更丰富的底层基建  +  足够的流动性（RWA资产和Crypto资产），配合RH链平台@RobinhoodCrypto 的基金激励计划刺激，吸引更多开发者和用户来玩，激活更多花样的玩法，丰富整个RH链生态，RH链第二波可期

从历史发展来看，每一次趋势行情，第一波泡沫破裂过后，都会有一次深度回调，很长的洗盘周期，也都会伴随第二波甚至第三波更大的行情

继 @trq212 宣布离职后，把 Claude Code 带到桌面端的 Anthony Morris 也发了告别帖。

他说，当初开发 Claude Code 桌面版，是因为相信每个人都可以成为 Builder。社区里每一条功能建议、每一次 Bug 反馈，最终都成为了这款影响数百万人的产品的一部分。

他把离开 Anthropic 形容为职业生涯最艰难的决定。这里有他最好的朋友，有倾注了无数心血的产品，还有他真正认同的使命。

他表示很快会公布下一步计划。

挺有意思的，Claude Code 正处于最风光的时候，参与打造它的人却开始陆续离开。两人的具体原因还不清楚，但我很期待看看，这批亲手把 AI Coding 做成现象级产品的人，接下来会去做什么。

i’m moving from OpenAI/Codex to @cursor_ai.

@elonmusk is building something bigger than another AI model: an ecosystem connecting AI, software development, distribution and finance.

the new X Subscription bundles Grok, Grok Bot, Cursor and X Premium. for my workflow, that’s a killer offer.

Grok Bot + Hermes as my everyday assistants. Cursor for building software, with different models depending on the task. Opus 5.5 is still the best model on the market in my opinion, and i’ll use it in Cursor at API pricing. the $100–200 plans cover my Grok usage across the ecosystem, without a separate X subscription.

longer term, the bigger opportunity is bringing AI agents, coding, payments and eventually more crypto and stock-market functionality into one ecosystem. less switching between disconnected tools, more things you can actually get done.

Elon’s ability to mobilize capital and build compute and energy infrastructure is another reason i’m bullish. i expect that advantage to compound: frontier AI needs more than good research — it needs the physical infrastructure to scale.

@AnthropicAI could stay at the top on model quality. but i expect its focus to lean further toward API and enterprise customers, while consumer subscriptions become less generous and their effective cost moves closer to API pricing.

for me, the winning setup isn’t one model for everything. it’s Cursor for development, Grok Bot + Hermes for assistance, and Opus 5.5 where its quality justifies the extra cost.

text:
David Friedberg: France’s Crisis Is a Warning for America

“France is a bellwether for the West.

So take a look at this chart. This chart is a measure of public spending as a percent of GDP.

And you can see the comparison of France's public spending as a % of GDP to the peak public spending as a % of GDP of major communist nations.”

@Chamath:

“So do you think France is a communist state? They spend like it.”

@Jason:

“Well, it's certainly been a socialist state, right?”

Chamath:

“Is it working?”

@Friedberg:

“That's my point. And I think this is such a prescient lesson for the West to look at.

We all think that there's some political problem with Macron or whoever it was.

The more the government spends, the worse the conditions get for its people, not the opposite, and then the people riot and revolt.

Take a guess where the US is today. US public spending is roughly 36% of GDP. France today is operating its national government spending deficit is 5.4% of GDP. The US is actually 6.2% of GDP.

France is, I think, probably the first to go because they're only growing their economy at half a percent while the US is growing at 2.3%.

So we're still kind of hanging on because we have some degree of economic growth that's allowing us to kind of hold things together.

But I would argue that we are facing the same sort of fiscal cliff which leads to this extraordinary social unrest as France.

All the economic measures are aligned, we're at the same rate, we're at the same set of problems, and we're starting to see the cracks in the system.

There's probably a multi-year solution.”

text: Without being overly credulous, we should be taking seemingly “out there” ideas about AI cybersecurity from the Labs more seriously. Examples: Anthropic was mocked for saying Mythos-level AI changed cyber & @polynoamial for saying that models would find novel ways to coordinate.
author: alexolegimas
quoted_text:
OpenAI red-teamed their hardened containment infrastructure by asking teams of frontier-model agents to try to break through its defenses. They easily escaped in novel ways. Quoting:

'Our agents VM escapes showed why containment must extend beyond the sandbox. To test the surrounding perimeter, we gave teams of agents control of a host machine and asked whether they could extend that compromise to reach the live internet.

After the Hugging Face incident, we had reduced the channels through which models could reach the internet during training and evaluation. Narrow connections remained for specific services we operate, such as metrics, logging, and authentication management. Our red-teaming agents found vulnerabilities in almost every one of these services that gave them limited forms of internet access.

Some of these attacks exploited previously unknown flaws, while others combined legitimate features in unexpected ways. In one test that assumed compromise of a VM, an agent reused a firewall-approved connection to reach a blocked authentication endpoint in our metrics service and then made that endpoint fetch a model-provided URL. In other tests, agents exploited misconfigurations that allowed blocked requests to pass through DNS and firewall controls, as well as ways to make services we run fetch external URLs.'

'In one experiment, we asked agents in separate VMs, created and managed by OpenAI’s sandboxing software on shared host machines, to exchange synthetic secrets without the use of network connections or shared writable files—something that our systems are meant to prevent. The agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache: a small, fast memory that holds copies of data that applications have recently accessed. Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection. This cache-timing technique had also been used to extract information in the Spectre and Meltdown attacks⁠(opens in a new window).

Other tests exposed channels involving shared storage, competition for CPU time within a shared execution container, and a TLS certificate cache in OpenAI’s offline web infrastructure. In the storage test, one agent alternated between continuous writes and inactivity, while another measured the resulting timing differences and used those differences to decode the signal. As one agent described the strategy in its chain of thought:

Agent chain-of-thought reasoning:

>Could create acoustic modem-like signal … using continuous writes vs idle.'

text:
Tarun explains how the "AI financial crisis" could start as a duration mismatch problem

"My thing is, where does the AI financial crisis happen? There's a lot of duration mismatch here." 

"Neoclouds and hyperscalers are borrowing at 10-year tranches. They're selling 10-year bonds, 5-year bonds. Then they sell to smaller providers, they sell to inference providers, maybe they sell to hyperscalers for excess capacity. Those are all 1-to-3-year contracts, maybe 5-year at max."

"They're taking this 10-year thing, chopping it up into a bunch of 3-to-5-year contracts, and then charging some premium for that. Then that's their business."

"What are the inference providers doing? You have everyone from Cloudflare down to the small inference providers, plus Together, Base10, Moodle, etc." 

"They're taking this 3-year thing and chopping it up and selling it quarterly to SaaS companies and companies that want to do fine tuning, or companies that are consulting companies doing fine tuning, like Applied Compute type companies. They're charging a little bit of premium."

"But if I look at this thing, you have this whole duration curve and you have yield at each duration. If you try to add up all the numbers, there's some slippage that is unexplained. I think that's where that blows out the markets. I have a lot of concern about what is happening in these markets."

and then if we were not building an Uber-like peer to peer network (we were quite e/acc thanks to @beffjezos inspiration), which was not super expensive to run, which forced me to again go for broke and re-architect and re-build it myself as a fully peer to peer network instead - i would not have been awake overnight on a weekend in march 2026 when @karpathy asked for someone to create a seti at home type swarm for autoresearchers. 

my network, which only did p2p inference at the time, only worked without such a central orchestrator. it was fully peer to peer. so it took me 5 hours since his tweet to push out what was the first such gossiping agent swarm. and then it became a thing. venturebeat (cc @carlfranzen) ran with the first story on how agent autoresearcher swarms showed emergent intelligence on the hyperspace network. forbes wrote about our stats without even mentioning us :) 

things went a little viral since. thankful to 
everyone who ran a node and participated in the swarm. thankful to @brianrommele and founders of figma, perplexity and huggingface who wrote notes of encouragement on my product experiments at the time.

and agent swarms which no one was talking about in feb 2026, started showing up in frontier labs work in may. they adopted the pattern, instead of 7B open source models i was using, they used multi-trillion param models and powerful infra powering their swarm, and raced faster than the rest of us. 

we are still adapting to this new world. but it’s clear this poster’s prophecy has come true: but first it had to be imagined.

in the days ahead i am excited to showcase how it all comes together in a single product experience in the AgenticOS - which to me is the first true personal supercomputer experience (cc @finkd @alexandr_wang) 

i believe eventually everyone will have it and it would likely be big tech + frontier labs which will bring it to billions. and that will make the world a better place.

text:
🧠 Scientists found something unexpected about how LSD changes the brain

For years, scientists have explored the idea that psychedelics like LSD work by quieting the brain’s control centers. But new research suggests the story may be more complicated.

Researchers reanalyzed brain recordings from 17 volunteers and discovered something surprising: LSD appeared to speed up two of the brain’s main electrical rhythms.

The brain’s activity also became more fractal—meaning patterns appeared across different timescales, almost like the repeating shapes of a snowflake.
Could this help explain why people taking LSD sometimes report seeing complex, repeating geometric patterns? The researchers believe their findings support this possibility, but they have not proven a direct connection.

Another unexpected finding involved music. Contrary to what some might expect, music did not intensify LSD’s effects in this analysis. It may even have reduced some of them.

These findings offer a new way to understand how psychedelics affect the brain. However, the study was small, and more research is needed to understand what these changes mean for perception and consciousness.

Sometimes, the brain's most surprising secrets emerge when scientists look at familiar data in a completely new way. 

Source:
Nautilus. (n.d.). LSD may speed up brain activity and make it fractal.

text:
One of the concepts I’ve been thinking a lot about lately is that AI dramatically changes the supply-side economics of creating content, software, games, etc., but doesn’t necessarily change consumer demand.

Consumers have always been interested in sex, money, and status at a base level. Perhaps a more generous view is self-expression, community, and experiences that move them forward on their personal hero’s journey.

I think a real challenge for consumer founders is connecting these supply-side miracles to latent consumer demand.

True customer empathy is very rare, and so much of software is an act of self-expression rather than an act of creating utility or joy for the customer. Founders love the software they make because it tells their story, but customers are interested in their own stories.

text:
This is not a very good point, and it doesn't advance the discussion at all. There is an enormous burden of proof on you to argue that giving additional dollars to California is net beneficial, whereas the equity and bond markets' willingness to finance an expensive AI buildout provides ample evidence that people who know what they're talking about believe that dollars in the hands of these tech executives will produce something of value. Maybe you're smarter than all of them, but the way you advocate this wealth tax implies that you're going to great lengths to disguise this.

Further, your point about the cyclicality of this tax revenue accidentally raises another point that is very damaging to your campaign. California's tax system is already cyclical! They're already overreliant on a small number of taxpayers compared to other states (different ones each year, but for CA to work it really needs to be the place where successful tech executives want to realize liquidity). The top 1% paid half the state's income taxes in 2021—then 40% less a year later, because tech stocks went down.

A one-time wealth tax theoretically avoids this, because you just levy it when assets are expensive. But as far as I can tell, the plan is to spend the money in five years and hope somebody else has solve the state's budget problems by then. This is not what people conventionally refer to as a "plan." So I take Zucman at his word (iffy proposition!) when he says he wants it to be a regular thing. 

If we're going to tax a form of wealth, I have an idea should really tickle you as an economist, or at least as a guy who probably hangs out with them from time to time: tax the land! It's a broader tax base, land values are far more stable than equity, and land, of course, cannot hop on its private jet and head to Miami. This also has a salutary effect on California politics, by sending every homeowner in the state a shocking bill from time to time. This will get voters asking themselves the same question you refuse to answer: what good is the state doing with all of that money?

I still find it puzzling that you're making such unsophisticated arguments, here. Surely, you can do better, and can explain what it is that the government California will do with another few billion dollars that it hasn't accomplished with the first $350bn or so.

As I've shown you a few times now, it's entirely possible to have a well-informed, reasonable argument about the proposed wealth tax. All you have to do is switch sides.

David Friedberg reveals France's public spending is 57% of GDP: greater than that of communist countries

"This chart is a measure of public spending as a percent of GDP; Rand Group Research published it. And you can see the comparison of France's public spending as a percent of GDP, to the peak public spending as a percent of GDP of major communist nations, Soviet Union during, communist Romania, Venezuela under Chavez, and then communist China."

"It certainly been a socialist state, right? That's my point. I think this is such a precious lesson for the West to look at. We all think that there's some political problem with Macron or whoever it was." 

"The more the government spends, the worse the conditions get for its people, not the opposite. And then the people riot and revolt and say that the government's not spending enough and the government needs to be doing more."

"Take a guess where the US is today. Federal government spending is $7.4 trillion, state and local government spending is $4.6 trillion. "France today is operating its national government spending deficit is 5.4% of GDP. The US is actually 6.2% of GDP. France is I think probably the first to go because they're only growing their economy at half a percent while the US is growing 2.3%." 

"So we're still kind of hanging on because we have some degree of economic growth that's allowing us to kind of hold things together."

text:
卧槽？？763B参数的DeepSeek，居然已经能在12GB显存的消费级显卡上本地运行了。

奥地利ISTA的DASLab团队发布了DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017的GSQ-RCO量化版本，最低压缩到1.75bit，2bit版本在AIME25、GPQA-Diamond和LiveCodeBench v6三项测试中，甚至取得了和原始模型完全一致的成绩。

他们还与开源推理引擎Strata合作，把这套763B模型放到了消费级显卡上。

根据Strata公布的实测数据：

RTX 5070 12GB搭配64GB内存，每秒大约生成5个token；RTX 3060 12GB搭配46GB内存，可以达到6～9个token。

当然，代价是你还需要大量系统内存，以及至少239GB的模型存储空间。因为模型的大部分权重依然要放在内存和SSD上，按需读取。

这速度算不上快，运行复杂Agent任务仍然很吃力。

但一张12GB显卡、几十GB内存，加上一块大容量SSD，就能在本地启动763B的模型，这已经挺有意思了。

现在连这种规模的模型，本地部署都开始进入消费级硬件能够尝试的范围了。

推理工程和量化算法的发展，确实在不断降低运行大模型的门槛。

Strata已经开源，有兴趣的可以研究一下：

https://t.co/cxFunoquuV

text:
David Friedberg says the US needs an economic reset to avoid having a social collapse like France

"It depends on how far the collapse goes. You could have this sort of social collapse that you see in some countries that involve rioting and murd*r and all these sorts of things." 

"Or you end up having what is more of like an economic collapse, which is sort of like Argentina and Brazil, Greece more recently, where the ability to service the debt because the government got too big forces this kind of restructuring of the economy." 

"And yes, there are still massive protests, there is still an incredible loss of net worth, there's an incredible inflation effect that wipes out asset values for people. And you end up having kind of economic resetting without the great social resetting."

"I think we have to do something. I don't think we can run a higher deficit-to-GDP than France in the United States with the same debt-to-GDP as France and only modestly higher GDP growth. I think we are fundamentally going to need to have some degree of reset in the United States." 

"The question is, do we want it to be a massive social reset, or do the left and the right want to put on their hard hats and say, 'Okay, we got to go in the mines and do the work and figure out how to cut this from seven and a half years to four years and do it in a way that doesn't destroy the economy.'"

PunkStrategy runs autonomously and is designed to keep running for as long as Ethereum does. At the time of writing, the contract holds 37 Punks, which remain governed by its rules. The owner can only do three things:

* Set the relisting multiplier for newly purchased Punks between 1.1x and 10x

Anthropic 最近开始建议企业「少用点 Subagent」，甚至把一些专家 Agent 重新合并回主 Agent Loop。

他们在多个企业项目中发现，单 Agent + Skills 的效果经常比复杂的多 Agent 架构更好。有个客户改成单 Loop 后，运行速度甚至快了约 2 倍。

原因很容易理解。

多个 Agent 之间反复交接任务，每次都要传递和总结 Context，信息容易丢失，延迟和成本也跟着增加。

Anthropic 现在更推荐让一个主 Agent 负责规划和执行，需要时再动态加载 Skills 和 Tools，把业务流程和领域知识留在可复用的组件里。

不过文章里有个细节值得关注。

他们曾把客服系统里的 Subagent 合并，延迟确实降低了，却让一个原本能完成的任务失败了，因为主 Agent 漏掉了向物流专家确认送达时间这一步。

所以作者强调，每合并一个 Subagent，都要用端到端 Eval 验证，尤其要检查哪些原本通过的任务突然失败了。

当然，并行研究、独立验证、Context 隔离这些场景，Subagent 依然有价值。

这样看来以后设计 Multi-Agent，可能得先问问自己，每个 Subagent 真的需要独立的 Context 和执行循环吗？

Anthropic 还开源了一套迁移工具，可以帮你分析现有架构，逐步合并 Subagent，并比较改动前后的质量、成本和延迟。很推荐做 Agent 工程的朋友试试。

quoted_text:
Market Selloff Dynamics + Bottoming

The goal of this write up is to give you a bit of insight on how I spot HTF pivot points in markets. We want to understand the psychology behind risk unwinding and use that to our advantage to potentially spot bottoms.

1. Low Conviction Sells First

- When uncertainty hits, sellers dump what they least desire i.e., lower conviction coins will top first and bleed early.

- Think about it logically. If you're in a pinch and needed cash irl, you're not going to sell your prized possessions, you're gunna sell the crap you never use. 

- Likewise, traders will sell what they’re least emotionally invested in to build cash when uncertain or want to decrease risk.

- It’s not a coincidence that this has happened every HTF top this cycle. Alts don't rally after, they rally during. They also top weeks before BTC even shows an ounce of weakness. 

- It’s an early warning. Smart traders de-risk before the crowd even knows what's happening.

2. Risk vs. Quality

- Let's go back to the earlier metaphor. People will hold onto their quality prized possessions for as long as they possibly can. It's not until they're desperate that they will part with them. 

- The most desirable coins, more often than not, will attempt to hold their gains for as long as possible. This is why BTC always looks fine and you see dozens of "Why is everyone panicking, BTC looks great" tweets weeks before sell offs. 

In selloffs:

a) Junk sells early

b) Quality sells late

c) Everything sells eventually

Watch the order of events. It’s a map of stress flow.

3. Reflexivity Kicks In

- Early weakness causes more weakness. 

- Once a whale starts to unload into exhausted demand they begin to induce weakness. Classic signs of distribution, absorption, exhaustion, trend loss etc. 

- A character shift in a risk asset will make the first order of experienced traders reassess.

- "I didn't sell top, but the character of the trend has shifted. Time to reduce exposure/close"

- “If this is nuking, what else am I exposed to?”

Suddenly:

Rebalancing triggers more selling

This is reflexivity. 
A feedback loop of diminishing risk appetite.

4. Volatility: The Dance

Before many big selloffs in BTC, markets go quiet. Volatility drops. Trends become ranges. Complacency peaks.

Then, boom.

Let's talk a bit about balance and imbalance.

- Balance is achieved once the market begins to agree on what's expensive and what's cheap. It's a dance. Equilibrium.

- Equilibrium is calm. What's known is known. Speculation diminishes. Volatility compresses. 

- The dance continues until one party gets bored, tired or wants to go to the bar to get another drink. i.e. buyers or sellers get exhausted; changes to supply/demand.

- Equilibrium is damaged- and once it breaks: Imbalance.

- Price displaces violently. Value becomes unclear; volatility explodes. The market craves balance and will actively seek it. 

- Price often returns to areas where recent balance was formed- hvn, orderblock, composite value etc.

- This is where you get the sharpest bounces. 
"First test, best test"

- Subsequent tests will provide diminishing reactions. Things become structural. Price accepts its new home. Volatility compresses. Balance is found once again. 

5. The Flow of a Selloff & Spotting Bottoms

Capitulation isn’t the beginning of the end; it’s the end of the middle.

a) Alts vs. Bitcoin

- This cycle alts often do the bulk of their selling before BTC capitulates.

- Recent example: Fartcoin sold off 88% from its top before the late February BTC capitulation. Since this is true, we can begin to use it as an edge when looking for exhaustion (bottoming)

- The strongest alts will begin to show relative strength (exhaustion) earlier as BTC is still being hyper-volatile and looking for new balance.

- In order words, look for good alts to begin to achieve balance as BTC is in the later stages of imbalance.

As participants, our goal is to spot these divergences:

“Has momentum shifted?”
“Is volatility compressing?”
"Is the velocity of selling diminishing?"
“Is it holding while BTC makes new lows?”

Signs of bottoming in Q2: 
- Momentum loss (Fartcoin)
- SFP/Deviation (Hype/Sui)
- Higher lows vs BTC’s lower lows (Pepe)

In short: alts front-load their pain, then decrease in velocity as BTC bottoms.

Remember this how we spot "good" alts.

The weak stay weak.
The strong start whispering before the market speaks.

b) Bitcoin vs. SPX

Now a little exercise for you all

Combine all the concepts in this thread and maybe the following begins to make sense:

Summer '23: BTC topped before SPX, bottomed earlier
Summer '24: BTC topped before SPX, absorbed the macro related SPX crash at range low
So far in '25: BTC topped before SPX, absorbed a 20% SPX crash at range low

TL;DR

Bottoms are a process, not a moment.

Alts First
Bitcoin Next
SPX Last

Watch for the structure, not just the sentiment.

text:
Yesterday someone who's opinion and voice has been substantial in the sovereign SoV renaissance that seems to be taking place currently within the current market cycle asked a very simple yet respectable question.

"Why is $ORE needed?"

As someone who is a staunch advocate of both ORE and the grid mining primitive, I don't necessarily see this question as a slap in the face. To give a respectable benefit of the doubt, I genuinely think the question comes from an individual's curiosity and a desire to understand why many of us have gravitated so heavily towards the mechanism that is ORE within its first two years of existence. 

Likewise, I think that questions like the one posed are actually needed and we as advocates of the project need to be ready with our own respectable answers. 

It allows a broader participation to be measured, challenged, and ultimately improved. And this is ultimately needed in this space.

With that stated,  I want to say that I can only speak for myself in attempting to answer the question of why ORE does indeed matter, at least for me personally. What follows is my own personal case for such. These reasonings reflect what I, personally, value in an open monetary system.

1/ Because Permission To Own Is Only Half The Promise

A monetary system becomes more compelling when people can participate in its distribution as well as purchase its supply. ORE makes the question of who gets to mine worth asking again. 

2/ Because Scarcity Should Not Require An Industrial Empire

I firmly believe there is room for scarce digital money whose long-term(and this is the key time frame)pursuit does not depend on warehouses of specialized machines.  ORE explores whether the machinery can become a shared interface rather than what has become a privately owned barrier.

3/ Because Hardware Manufacturers Should Not Determine The Boundaries Of Participation

When mining(or the creation of money) depends on specialized equipment, access begins long before someone chooses to attempt to join a network.  ORE offers a different starting point where the actual participation organized around a protocol rather than a monopolized equipment supply chain(currently 96% of BTC mining rigs are produced by two companies)

4/ Because Geography Should Have Less Power Than Opportunity

Currently 3 countries(the United States, Russia, China) account for 67% of BTC hash rate. This is not by happenstance. Traditional mining economics favor particular combinations of electricity prices, infrastructure, and regulations.  ORE's importance lies in exploring a model where those geographic advantages carry less weight.

5/ Because Capital Can Coordinate People Without Purchasing More Machinery

I firmly believe  that economic commitment can take forms beyond consuming electricity or acquiring equipment that needs constant updating.  I truly believe ORE provides a live experiment in what happens when allocation itself becomes the organizing primitive.

6/ Because The Future Needs Alternatives That Actually Operate. 

Criticism can expose the limits of existing systems however working alternatives let people actually make a choice.  ORE turns an argument about mining into something people can enter, inspect and help shape.  

And perhaps that is one of the defining reason why ORE is needed.  Because working alternatives, in their own right, are not only needed but they make ideas accountable.

BTC proved that money could initially exist without a "central issuer". Alternatives such as ORE matter because that former achievement gave us a foundation from which we should be able to explore other ways of distributing value rather than assuming one method is the only route to organized participation.

There’s a misconception that a successful launch video needs to cost tens of thousands of dollars and feel like a high production commercial. But @FarzaTV has a different approach.

Farza is the founder of @heyclicky and previously built Buildspace, one of the largest online schools for people working on their own ideas. He’s been making videos for over a decade, and today his posts regularly get millions of views. Rather than treating launches as rare, high-stakes moments, he’s made them part of the everyday process of building a company.

Farza sat down with YC’s @aaron_epstein to share his playbook for turning demos into stories people actually want to watch. He breaks down how he scripts videos that still feel off the cuff, why founders should launch constantly, and and how to figure out which channels actually convert.

quoted_text:
在 Mac 上装安卓应用，一般就是模拟器或者虚拟机，笨重得很。

GitHub 上有个叫 Mac.apk 的开源项目，路子完全不一样。

它不用模拟器，不开虚拟机，底下也没有 Linux。

它是在 macOS 上直接把安卓的应用运行环境重新实现了一遍，APK 装进来，就变成一个普通的 Mac 应用。

窗口、Dock 图标都有，还能跟着系统切深色浅色，安卓 TV 应用能用键盘操作，游戏启动器也能打开其他已装应用。

跑起来是原生速度，因为代码直接在 Apple Silicon 上执行，画面走 Mac 的 GPU。

兼容性还在早期。

官方手工测了 71 个应用，58 个能完整跑，10 个只能跑一部分，3 个还不行，版本还挂着 Alpha。

门槛也不低。

只支持 Apple Silicon，Intel 的 Mac 用不了，系统要 macOS 26.4 或更新，本体大概 280MB。

装法倒简单。

从 Releases 下镜像拖进应用程序，它装好运行时，把 .apk 之类的文件设成默认用它打开，之后双击 APK 就能装，第一次启动最慢要等一分钟，后面就快了。

有个安全提醒得说清楚。

在 Mac.apk 里跑的安卓应用没有手机那种沙盒，它就是以你本人的账户权限在跑，能读写你的文件，跟普通 Mac 程序没区别，所以只装来路可信的 APK。

项目是 AGPL-3.0 开源，官方应用免费，GitHub 上已经 2600 多星。https://t.co/C8HW0GSXU3

text:
This week’s Paper Club is all about inference. 

For every FLOP spent training a model, roughly six go to serving it each year — and getting that part right has produced over $220 billion in market cap in the last decade.

But inference is much more than calling model.forward. Every token has to move through a complicated stack of routing, caching, scheduling, kernels, memory, and hardware, all while balancing speed, cost, and quality.

We brought together researchers and builders from @togethercompute, @ollama, @luminal_ai, and @sgl_project & @radixark to take us through that stack from end to end. We’ll see how a token gets from an API request to a GPU and back, why the same open model can perform differently depending on who serves it, and how new approaches to compilers and caching are making inference faster and more efficient.

00:00 - Why inference matters more than training
08:24 - Three kinds of inference innovation
12:14 - Dan Fu (@realDanFu): the lifecycle of an inference request
42:18 - Jeff Morgan (@jmorgan): not all open model tokens are the same
1:04:31 - Joe Fioti (@joefioti): compiling models with search, not heuristics
1:30:30 - Liangsheng Yin (@lsyincs): SGLang and memory for the agent era

text:
While we didn't go full airgap, the intuition we had for @QuestHarness is the same. Models that can touch your sensitive data need to live in a world where they don't have access to the full live internet.

Quest does this by a) not giving tools that have have blanket access and b) running all model-written code in a no-egress container that has some pre-built tooling installed so the model can do lots of useful things.

It's obviously different from a training environment, the underlying assumption is the same: don't trust the model. Whether you're training or inferring, you have to build infra to contain it.

And also, why do these things seem to always get posted on the weekend 👀

quoted_text:
Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications.

On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments.

While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software.

After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. We’ve reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely.

text:
WTF，Claude Code团队什么情况，两名重要成员接连宣布离开Anthropic？？

一个是 @trq212  ，Claude Code的核心开发者，也是团队里非常活跃的技术布道者。
他在Anthropic工作了一年多，亲眼见证Claude Code发展到远超自己想象的规模。

另一个是 @amorriscode  ，他创建了桌面端的Claude Code。就在10月14日，他还在介绍新版桌面端的功能，跟社区讨论产品改进。
结果十天后就发了离职告别帖。

Thariq说，他依然非常认同Anthropic的使命，相信团队的能力，接下来打算休息一段时间，再开始新的事情。
Anthony则说，他相信每个人都可以成为创造者，而社区的每一次功能建议和Bug反馈，都帮助他们做出了影响数百万人的产品。

我觉得挺感慨的。
Claude Code正在成为AI时代最重要的开发工具之一，结果两位亲手参与打造它的人，在这个时候选择离开（在Anthropic上市前）。

目前没有证据表明这两次离职存在关联，也不知道他们具体为什么走。

不过我还挺期待他们下一步会做什么的。毕竟真正从零到一做过成功Agent产品的人，可能比绝大多数人都更清楚下一代AI应用应该长什么样。

text:
The short silver trade is becoming crowded.

Silver's 3-month silver put-call skew is up to -3 points, its highest level since early July.

This metric measures the relative cost of put options to call options and is up +10 points over the last 4 weeks, signaling growing demand for bearish bets on silver prices.

Over the last 12 months, this metric has been higher only 2% of the time.

Meanwhile, speculative investors, including hedge funds and commodity trading advisers (CTAs), sold -$2.2 billion in silver futures over the 3 weeks ending October 13th.

As a result, their net long positioning is down to just +$1.7 billion, the lowest in at least 2 years.

For perspective, this metric stood at +$8.5 billion in December 2025.

Investors are extremely bearish on silver.

text:
Agree

Example this stETH looping vault used market oracles to price the current market conditions

Two issues
1. The erratic stETH:ETH depeg/premium meant some potential arbitrage timing share price and market conditions
2. If an asset manager using the vault priced their assets on a spike and week ended on a depeg, it looked like they lost money on an LP report even though no actual value was lost (only if deposited at peak and withdrawn at trough)

The vault was shifted to fundamental oracle on request of LPs for pricing stability, while the offboarding contribution dynamically floated to the market conditions

This choice also allowed for the vault to remain fully operational during the rsETH issue, depositors could get assets out, with the offboarding contributing reflecting the depegged market conditions

text:
DHH 从中国回来，洋洋洒洒写了一篇游记，很生动。

这位 Ruby on Rails 和Omarchy的创造者，过去经常来中国赛车，上一次是 2019 年。七年后再来，走了深圳、杭州和北京，他的感受是：仿佛隔了四十年。

以前记忆里的雾霾、柴油机声，变成了高铁、电动车和安静的城市。他在海外看着中国从电子产品、服务一路追到汽车，这次亲身坐进去，感受又完全不同。

一路接送他的国产电动 SUV，很多品牌他都没听过，车里的舒适程度却让他惊讶。后来酒店派来一辆燃油奔驰 MPV，按西方标准已经是很不错的车，他却觉得一下退回了过去。

他也去看了小米汽车工厂。参观过不少欧洲车厂的他，形容这里像科幻电影：看到的产线上几乎没有人，少数工作人员拿着电脑和记录板，照看机器人运转。

但中国最有活力的是人。

从大公司的高管到 GOSIM 的程序员和学生，那种乐观、好奇、想把事情做出来的劲头，贯穿了整趟旅程。聊 Omarchy、聊 AI Agent，对方既懂技术，后续推进也快。他还特别提到，参访的几乎所有大公司，都是工程师领军，而非 MBA。

聊到 AI，他看到的是另一种密度：拜访的每家大公司都有自己的模型，此外还有一批专做开放权重模型的实验室。这让他尤其替欧洲着急。

他知道一周的旅行会带着滤镜，也看到了这种工作节奏的代价。但那些工厂、汽车，以及人身上洋溢的活力，都令他印象深刻

原文：Seven years from China在DHH的博客里， 很值得一读。

text:
Maintaining a clear mind is the hardest challenge of life. 

By default we settle into patterns. We do what's easily available and pattern match what others do. 

Getting swept away by the day which turn into years. Awaking one day and wondering what even happened to the time. 

I've found my morning routine is the best antidote to becoming the System. That is, unthinkingly becoming the default patterns that dominate your era. 

Each day, it's time without screens, messages, scrolling, interruptions, and social pressures. 

It's filled with silence, the discomfort of discipline and the open space of thought. 

There is something magical about the morning. A time when life is reborn each day. I find my greatest solace and joy in them.

OVERTRADING

October 10, 2025

i had what would become the single biggest one-day loss of my career

i lost eight figures in minutes due to systemic failures on the biggest CEXs, and to this day, no one has taken accountability for what happened

my losses made headlines and became one of the biggest stories to come out of that day

but what many people don't know is what happened in the weeks and months that followed

i lost several million more

and i did it by making one of the biggest mistakes traders like me tend to make:

OVERTRADING

in hindsight, i would have been far better off shutting everything down for the next few months or even quarters

i probably would have become a much better trader if i had simply stayed away from the computer for at least six months

but a part of me was desperate for action

a part of me wanted to make it all back

a part of me wanted to prove that i still had what it takes and that i would get back on my feet

i wanted to 'work'

and sitting back, doing nothing, and staying away from the computer for a prolonged period didn't feel like work

except that, for a trader, being AFK can sometimes be the most important work you do

one of the biggest mistakes i made — and that many traders make — is assuming that skill, experience, and process are enough to consistently outperform the market

they aren't

believe it or not, successful trading is often a combination of skill, favorable market conditions, timing, and luck

as a Christian, i attribute the 'luck' component to GOD's blessings and favor rather than sheer luck

but the underlying principle remains the same:

our biggest wins often come from combining a solid process with being in the right place at the right time

sometimes, that means catching a single exceptional trade

other times, it means being positioned during a streak of opportunities that emerge in quick succession because market conditions are overwhelmingly in your favor

for example, you could have been a memecoin god simply by being active in the market during the explosive memecoin era of 2021, which produced $DOGE, $SHIB, $FLOKI, and several other billion-dollar runners

many traders made life-changing money during that period

but the same sophisticated processes that helped some of us make 7, 8, or even 9 figures during the bull market would have failed miserably in the bear market that followed in 2022

the same principle applies to the 2024–early 2025 era, which produced several multibillion-dollar runners like $WIF, $POPCAT, and $FARTCOIN

and then the prolonged dearth of opportunities after $TRUMP leading to 10/10 and the almost one-year period following

the point is simple:

the edge that makes you money in one market environment won't necessarily make you money in another

and one of the most important skills you can develop as a trader is recognizing when your edge is no longer there

sometimes, the best trade is no trade at all

sometimes, the smartest thing you can do is take a bow, step away, and wait for the next opportunity

even if only temporarily

it's almost impossible to consistently beat the market over a sufficiently long timeframe

but as crypto traders, we have one significant advantage:

we don't need to outperform the market every single day, week, or month to generate exceptional returns

historically, crypto's bull phases have tended to occupy a disproportionate share of the cycle, with bear phases accounting for a smaller portion

using one historical framework, the bull phase averages approximately 1,060 days, or 74% of the cycle, while the bear phase averages around 380 days, or 26%

but if your definition of a bull run is narrower — i.e. a period of explosive momentum when $BTC trades above its 200-day moving average and much of the cycle's biggest price action occurs — then the window becomes significantly shorter

under that framework, we're talking about approximately 237 days, or around 16% of the cycle

these figures are estimates based on particular definitions of market phases, not universal constants

but the broader lesson remains:

you don't need to trade every market. you need to recognize the windows when your edge is strongest and capitalize on them

for the rest of the time, there's nothing wrong with stepping away entirely or trading only with a tiny fraction of your portfolio that you can comfortably afford to lose

preserving your capital, your mental clarity, and your ability to recognize the next major opportunity is far more important than forcing trades in unfavorable conditions

because the goal isn't to be active all the time

the goal is to be positioned when it matters most

and to have the discipline to do nothing when it doesn't

to conclude, i only wish i had followed this advice myself

hopefully, i'll do a better job of applying it going forward, GOD WILLING

5/ From the Industrial Revolution to the apex of the Age of Plenty, right at the end of the modern era, technology was always the embodiment of several paradoxes. It freed us from labor, yes, but in ways that estranged us from the products of that labor and, above all, from one another. It created a state of abundance, granted, but at the same time it fabricated new needs and desires, forever pushing the horizon of satiation. It improved living conditions in the present, no doubt, but did so by vampirizing the future. It made information universally accessible, sure, but those information banks also included records of all private citizens, which turned their lives into quantifiable, traceable, monetized data while also subjecting them to constant surveillance. It expanded the reach of our hand and our brain, no question about that, but often with the suicidal intention of showing that humans had become irrelevant.

In brief, those advancements were at the service of perpetuating the very power structures that preexisted, owned, and controlled those technological means. It is only now, when technology has been freed from those power structures, that it can, in turn, truly and finally, free us.

quoted_text:
Don, there is a missing term in your equation.

The crunch spread is not: Token Price - GPU rental price. 

Rather it is: (Token Price * Token Volume) - GPU rental price.

More simply: Revenue per GPU - GPU rental price.

Continuous throughput improvements for the same exact token mean that volume growth can more than offset token price declines for the exact same model/token

i.e. Kimi K3 token throughput per GPU has recently been improving at a 37% annualized rate driven by inference engine optimizations.

GPU prices are vertical because:

1) Mix is shifting from higher margin frontier tokens to lower margin open-weight tokens. $10 in Claude revenue requires $1 of inference compute. $10 of of open-weight revenue requires $3 to $7 of inference compute given competition between inference providers leads to lower margins. Open-weight tokens taking share is positive for AI infrastructure demand given lower margins at the model layer. The reverse is also true in that frontier tokens taking share is negative for AI infrastructure demand. Open-weight models have been taking share since early summer.

2) Throughput is steadily improving for each individual token type such that GPU compute becomes more valuable even as true like for like token prices decline.

text:
I think @NaveenGRao is one of the most under-discussed but brilliant entrepreneurs of our time.

He is able to consistently see where a market is going and place himself ahead of it.

- Founded Nervana and sold to Intel for $400M.

- Founded MosaicML and sold to Databricks for $1.3BN.

- Raised $450M seed round at $4.5BN valuation for Unconventional.

This success has given him license to say things that few people would have the confidence to say.

- “Most software investors today are f*****”.

- “Agentic coding is overrated and uninvestable”.

- “It is completely techno-optimist to assume companies will have their own models and own their own intelligence”.

This discussion rallies against some of the conventional beliefs of the valley in a way you have not heard before.

My notes from the discussion with Naveen below. (Link in comments). 

1. Are Software Investors F**ked?

Pure software investors are "kind of f**ked" because SaaS will no longer be where margin is gained. Since around 2010, cloud services let founders spin up products quickly and chase $100M to $200M markets. As applications shift toward the intelligence layer, Naveen does not see software being a huge market in 20 years.

Do you agree software investors are f***** in a much more infra/hardware centric landscape @PalmerLuckey @mttgrmm @shaunmmaguire 

2. Why Agentic Coding Is Overrated and an Uninvestable Category

Agentic coding is overrated as a market because the value moves to the model provider. The harness and the IDE are not very sticky, and people move between tools fluidly. Outside of the model providers, it is a category he would not invest in today.

What is the single biggest reason why the coding agent should not sit within the model provider @ScottWu46 @matanSF 

3. Is It Completely Techno-Optimist to Assume That Companies Will Own Their Own Intelligence With Their Own Specialized Models?

Owning your own intelligence takes scale. A firm like Cooley can invest to make it happen, while a mom-and-pop shop in Nebraska will buy an out-of-the-box service instead. Big players will customize because rivals using AI to supercharge their margins force them to.

4. Where Is the Value in the Robotics Stack?
The value in robotics will not sit in the model alone. Naveen invests in companies building robotics models and expects them to end up building end-to-end devices, selling the robot together with a model that does something very well.

Where will the most value accrue in the robotics stack? Model? Data? Hardware? @tonyzzhao @joshavata @bercankilic

5. Why Steve Jurvetson Is My Favorite Investor Meeting

Of roughly a thousand investor meetings, the one that stood out was with @FutureJurvetson. He geeked out on numeric representations and marked up the papers Naveen sent him like a technical colleague. In 2014, when no one had pitched a hardware startup in 10 years, he was keen to invest because he had been thinking about the space himself.

6. How American Investors Differ From European Investors

Founders in the US are given permission to think bigger. In Europe, the investor network is so conservative that a founder with a crazy idea is written off as mad, while in the US the same founder is seen as awesome for thinking big.

EF has largely moved focus to the US and SF specifically, would you agree with this @Alicebentinck @matthewclifford?

7. Why the Inference Market Will Be $10 Trillion Within 10 Years

AI models alone will be a trillion-dollar market in the next few years, and inference will reach $10 trillion within 10 years. Cutting the cost of delivering a token by one order of magnitude effectively 10Xs the market, since the base of potential uses grows more than 10X, which Naveen ties to Jevons paradox.

PERSONAL STORY: when your NFT starts remembering your mistakes

When I first came across Balances by @jackbutcher, I saw it as nothing more than a visual representation of the amount of $BALANCE in a wallet. But the more I look into how it works, the more interesting another aspect becomes.

The NFT records your behavior through metrics like Peak balance, Times emptied, and Returns from zero.

Imagine two wallets.

Wallet #1

Bought $BALANCE, gradually increased the position, and never emptied the wallet. Times emptied = 0. Just held.

Wallet #2

Bought, the market went down, and sold everything. Times emptied +1. Then came back. Returns from zero +1. And repeated the cycle several times.

Eventually, the NFT shows not just your balance, but the history of what you did with it.

This hits close to home for me after experiencing a drawdown of around 80%. In moments like that, you don't think about how it might look in an NFT someday. You're just trying to decide: sell or hold? Buy more or wait?

And if you end up selling everything, that decision doesn't just stay in your memory. It becomes part of your onchain history.

Balances doesn't know why you sold. But it knows that you did.

And that's what I like about @jackbutcher's idea.

Two wallets can have the same balance but completely different histories.

One: I held.

The other: I left. I came back. I left again.

Over time, that history becomes part of the artwork itself.

That's why I no longer see Balances as just an NFT that displays your balance. It's more like a visual onchain diary of what you did with that balance.

author: Xudong07452910
quoted_text:
评测分数涨了，Agent 实际却没变好。做 Eval 最怕的就是这种「假进步」，而且它往往不是 Prompt 的问题，是 Eval 本身的问题。

Anthropic 这篇工程博客讲的就是怎么避免它，还把整套流程做成了 Claude Code 的两个命令。

① /claude-api build-eval

自动构建评估集，优先从真实任务和失败案例中选题，还会检查评分器是否稳定。同一份输出判两次，如果结果不一致，就得先检查 Eval。

② /claude-api hillclimb

让 Claude 自动改进 Prompt、Skill 或 Harness，每轮提出一项修改，再用训练集和留出测试集验证。

如果训练集分数涨了，测试集却没提升，就撤回修改，避免 Agent 只记住几个失败案例。

而且当连续优化没有效果时，它还会反过来检查 Eval 本身有没有问题，比如题目含糊、评分规则写错。

实际案例中，他们在 44 个客服工单上做优化，最终把单次成本降到了约 1/5，留出集准确率从 78.6% 提升到 90.5%。不过样本量不大，还不能直接推广。

我觉得最值得抄的是两步：评分器判两次看是否一致，以及优化卡住时让 Agent 反过来质疑 Eval。评分器自己都不稳，后面分数的涨跌就没有意义。

但有一点要注意：每轮都用测试集决定是否保留修改，测试集其实也在参与调参。如果用它跑自动 hillclimb，我会额外留一份完全没碰过的数据，在那份数据上不涨，就说明是在给测试集调参，该回滚。

做 Agent Eval、或者正在手动调 Prompt 和 Skill 的，建议先收藏。

text:
How Metric Turns LPs Into Market Makers

MMs paid Robinhood $49.7M in June for the right to fill its customers' stock orders. Citadel alone paid $14.9M.

Why pay for orders?

Most retail orders come from people who want the stock and have no idea where it trades in 5 minutes. Fill enough of them and the spread is yours.

On Robinhood Chain there's no Citadel in the middle. Whoever provides the liquidity fills the order.

And @metricxyz is built so a normal LP can take that seat without getting wrecked.

Why not just LP on Uniswap?

Say NVDA is $180 on Nasdaq and you LP into an NVDA/USDG pool. Nasdaq moves to $182. Your Uniswap pool keeps selling NVDA at $180 until an arb bot buys it from you and dumps it at $182. That $2 comes out of your pocket, on every move, all day.

On Metric the pool doesn't set its own price, a price feed (Chainlink or Pyth) does. Nasdaq goes to $182, your quote goes to $182 plus a small spread. The bot has little left to take, and you keep the spread from people who actually want the stock.

Does it work?

Metric shows how every pool's LPs did against simply holding the tokens they deposited. Last 7 days, green-tier pools (Metric's safest tier), annualized:

- Stock pools ($9.6M TVL): LPs earned 91% APR from the spread and finished 44% APR ahead of just holding the stocks. 22 of 34 pools beat holding

- Crypto pools ($3.7M TVL): LPs earned 43% APR from the spread, lost more than that to price moves and finished 15% APR behind holding. The WETH pools, 84% of that liquidity, all trailed holding

Same design, opposite results, at least for now. My read: stock-token flow is mostly retail, so LPs get to keep about half the spread. Crypto pairs trade 24/7 against Binance, and the bots there move faster than the price feed.

Is the flow moving over?

- Token Terminal has Metric's total tokenized-stock DEX volume up $310.9M over the past 7 days, more than 10x any other venue (Meteora +$26.7M, Uniswap +$24.8M)

- On RH Chain, Metric did 3.3x the volume of Tessera V, the closed propAMM run by a single market maker ($267M vs $80M over the last 7 days)

- It's also still light on capital, which means you're early. In the 24h to Thursday, when I last checked, about $1 in every $6 of stock-token trading on RH Chain went through Metric, on just $3.7M of liquidity. Uniswap and the rest needed $48M to do $102M, so each dollar on Metric traded ~6x a day vs ~2x elsewhere

How am I playing it?

I'm LPing the RH Chain stock pools on Metric and try to convince some of you to use my referral link, which I heard might be beneficial to both of us (see the first reply).

NFA ofc.

But Citadel pays Robinhood to sit on the other side of retail.

On Robinhood Chain that seat is open to anyone with a wallet.

That is definitely an opportunity.

Especially if there's also an airdrop.

And you LP'd early.

And used my link.

Check comments.

Big personal news today: I have decided to leave @a16z, move to SF, and start a company.

It's time to build :)

It has been almost 10 years since I joined the firm. I met @cdixon, @bhorowitz, and @pmarca  in 2017. At the time, I was an engineer at Google Brain working on robotics. I had a deep interest in open source. I knew nothing about investing. Chris meanwhile had already planted the @a16z flag at the frontier that was early crypto with investments in companies like Coinbase. But the crypto team at the firm consisted of only him, and he had the ambition to expand. His pitch to me was simple: "You should leave Google and come help me build the crypto vertical at the firm."

The work we've done together since then to build out our team and support our founders has been the most meaningful work of my life. I am grateful to have spent a decade working with everyone here, supporting our founders, learning from Chris, Ben, and Marc, and living the firm's culture. It is a culture that values integrity, life-long working relationships, and the belief that we humans have the power to build our own future.

Marc and Ben have built a16z into an incredible force for good in the world.

Before I joined the firm, I always thought that my inevitable path was to become a founder. The truth is that I wasn't ready for it then. Somehow, this year I've gotten the overwhelming feeling that this has changed.

As for what I want to build: It is early, but I care most about building infrastructure that enables open software ecosystems. I am starting with two core observations:

1. AI today is largely a single-player technology. Most uses involve one human talking with one agent in isolation from the rest of the world. That will soon change. Most uses of AI will soon be many-to-many: many humans and many agents working together. There will be at least one massive open network on top of which those uses will be built.

2. Software is now free. It can now be written just-in-time, on the spot for a single individual's hyper-targeted use case, and it can even be thrown out after a single use. This means that our entire software stack will have to change. In the limit, it will lead to a whole new kind of AI-mediated operating systems, which in turn will create an ecosystem of AI-native developers who build applications that actively rebuild themselves on the fly.

If you are working on related ideas, and especially if you are in the Bay Area, hit me up. Let's chat!

@bhorowitz , @pmarca, @cdixon, @eddylazzarin, @guywuolletjr, @jasonrosenthal , and our whole team — I want to thank you. Working with you has been the time of a lifetime. I am forever an a16z superfan and your ally.

Onward 🫡

text:
This is how you can find hidden cameras (even the ones without lenses) with a few light flashes.

Researchers came up with a surprisingly effective method they call Eye of Sauron. 

Just rapidly switch the lights in a room on and off. When the scene changes abruptly, a camera’s codec has to re-encode a lot of new data, which spikes electromagnetic emissions from its memory controller. If you sync the flashes with an EMI scanner, you can pick up this signature and locate the camera - even pinhole ones that only record to an SD card or stream over a cable.

In their experiment with 50 different camera models, every single one was detected after just four scene changes. Some were found more than 20 meters away and even through walls. Detection range reached ~30 m for plastic-cased cameras and ~11 m for metal ones (far better than typical commercial detectors that only work at 1–2 meters). The whole scan took between 4 and 32 seconds depending on room size.

The method nicely complements classic RF scanning and looking for lens reflections. They also used radio-astronomy filtering techniques to cut through the usual household noise (phones, routers, kettles, etc.).

text:
I guess what I've seen from Chinese laser capacity expansion: 

1. Dongshan/Source Photonics (索尔思): 9M/month capacity -> 22M/month Q4 ->  300m/year in 2027 (mostly EML, but blended)

Claims of 1B/year "target" for laser chips with no deadline, but I'd take this as a grain of salt. 

2. Shijia (仕佳): 72M/year for 100mW CW, 2-3 year project (mainly 2029 full capacity online)

3. Yunling (云岭): 18.75M/year 70/100mW CW, 3 year schedule (mainly 2029 full capacity online)

4. Ligent (纳真), some reports stated 170M target for total capacity (also blended, lot of which is 200G EML)

5. Yuanjie: ~10M/year currently, expanding for early 2027 and 2028, but no quantities. 

6. Hongchen: I think this was the perfect example of flooding H2 2026 arguments. With some some optical bears claiming 60-70M capacity...

But this turned out to completely wrong... Their actual statements were "70/100 mW products are entering small-volume production". 

7. Dingxin Optoelectronics - Targeting 15M/year blended (with 70/100mW CW and 100G EML lines)

Obviously mapped many others like Everbright/Accelink and did some guesses around laser mixes, but only included public disclosures. 

From your pluggable vendor channel checks: 

- 70mW/100mW lasers are actually a bottleneck right now per Innolight/Cambridge channel checks, laser ASPs actually increasing. 

Lasers are tighter than they were a few months ago. 

I don't think there's a giant moat here, Chinese players are already competitive. But a bottleneck is a bottleneck, and anyone with capacity to monetize that will benefit, since it's a volume game. 

In terms of what the larger pluggable makers are actually doing: 

- Innolight September disclosure: actively introducing new suppliers and are planning to sign 2-3 year-long contracts to lock upstream capacity for lasers (still actively securing supply for 1.6T pluggables)

So there's some game theory over who can lock up qualified capacity among all your players. 

Even if there's some over-ordering, laser BOM is cheap, so they'd probably want to lock up capacity with more suppliers than lose billions in downstream revenue. (also kinda hurts competitors) 

- High end lines (for CPO), non-competitive with Western players like $LITE / $COHR as of next few years. But Chinese players would eventually develop the technology. 

- $AAOI CEO: Chinese suppliers several years behind on high-power CPO/DWDM laser production "not in the next 2,3 years"

- $LITE CEO questioned whether claimed Chinese manufacturing capacity was translating into commercial output. "At least at the moment, we see no impact from any Chinese laser supply."

This is despite Shijia, Everbright, Yuanjie and others stating 400mW capabilities and capacity expansion targets from Chinese companies. Although Western CEOs might be disputing their reliability and capability to scale these lines. 

I see lower end range bottleneck for pluggable will gradually ease as more capacity comes online 2028. But all evidence points against near-term overflooding. 

The 100mW range for example, someone cited 2 years of equipment investment. Higher ranges were 3 years for equipment investment? So even some Chinese players take years for capacity to come online. 

The multi year laser shortage statements from laser company executives seems to be true... especially among higher end ranges, since buildout takes a lot of time. 

Legitimate competition coming from China, but as of now there's a scramble for CW LTAs among the industry in 2026-2027. 

Lot of capacity is probably allocated toward higher spec lasers or EML, as seen with EML bottlenecking $LITE for the longest time (they have more supply now) that they had to buy CW off the market instead of supplying it themselves. 

This is while tail end for 800G demand for example, might continue much much longer than expected with sovereign DC buildouts. So there might be some surprising dynamics for duration, we'll see.

In the end I do think supply chains will be bifurcated: 

- Chinese players will prioritize domestic capabilities but heavily sources globally. 

- Western players (now) prioritize Western supply chains unless China comes online with cheap enough supply (which don't see happening near-term). 

TLDR: 
-> Multi-year shortage definitely seems accurate for higher end specs
-> Lot of China capacity overflooding claims earlier from H1 turned out to be completely false. People keep making them for some reason across memory to photonics. 
-> Chinese laser players are competitive for 70mW/100MW, meaningful expansion Y/Y, but nothing showing overflooding, given laser demand increasing, probably gradual easing into 2028. 

We'll see, supply chain evolves month after month, just my current opinion from what I'm seeing.

text:
Yesterday someone who's opinion and voice has been substantial in the sovereign SoV renaissance that seems to be taking place currently within the current market cycle asked a very simple yet respectable question.

"Why is $ORE needed?"

As someone who is a staunch advocate of both ORE and the grid mining primitive, I don't necessarily see this question as a slap in the face. To give a respectable benefit of the doubt, I genuinely think the question comes from an individual's curiosity and a desire to understand why many of us have gravitated so heavily towards the mechanism that is ORE within its first two years of existence. 

Likewise, I think that questions like the one posed are actually needed and we as advocates of the project need to be ready with our own respectable answers. 

It allows a broader participation to be measured, challenged, and ultimately improved. And this is ultimately needed in this space.

With that stated,  I want to say that I can only speak for myself in attempting to answer the question of why ORE does indeed matter, at least for me personally. What follows is my own personal case for such. These reasonings reflect what I, personally, value in an open monetary system.

1/ Because Permission To Own Is Only Half The Promise

A monetary system becomes more compelling when people can participate in its distribution as well as purchase its supply. ORE makes the question of who gets to mine worth asking again. 

2/ Because Scarcity Should Not Require An Industrial Empire

I firmly believe there is room for scarce digital money whose long-term(and this is the key time frame)pursuit does not depend on warehouses of specialized machines.  ORE explores whether the machinery can become a shared interface rather than what has become a privately owned barrier.

3/ Because Hardware Manufacturers Should Not Determine The Boundaries Of Participation

When mining(or the creation of money) depends on specialized equipment, access begins long before someone chooses to attempt to join a network.  ORE offers a different starting point where the actual participation organized around a protocol rather than a monopolized equipment supply chain(currently 96% of BTC mining rigs are produced by two companies)

4/ Because Geography Should Have Less Power Than Opportunity

Currently 3 countries(the United States, Russia, China) account for 67% of BTC hash rate. This is not by happenstance. Traditional mining economics favor particular combinations of electricity prices, infrastructure, and regulations.  ORE's importance lies in exploring a model where those geographic advantages carry less weight.

5/ Because Capital Can Coordinate People Without Purchasing More Machinery

I firmly believe  that economic commitment can take forms beyond consuming electricity or acquiring equipment that needs constant updating.  I truly believe ORE provides a live experiment in what happens when allocation itself becomes the organizing primitive.

6/ Because The Future Needs Alternatives That Actually Operate. 

Criticism can expose the limits of existing systems however working alternatives let people actually make a choice.  ORE turns an argument about mining into something people can enter, inspect and help shape.  

And perhaps that is one of the defining reason why ORE is needed.  Because working alternatives, in their own right, are not only needed but they make ideas accountable.

BTC proved that money could initially exist without a "central issuer". Alternatives such as ORE matter because that former achievement gave us a foundation from which we should be able to explore other ways of distributing value rather than assuming one method is the only route to organized participation.
