text:
Was about to write this but Ben beat me to it. Econ is unique among the sciences in that it is several pretty different fields living under one umbrella. 

Empirical econ is the biggest subfield and its closest to biology or chemistry: it’s about designing or—even better—finding a natural experiment, or documenting interesting and important patterns in data. Most of the arguments in that field are about methods, eg do you have identification. More and more are starting to study AI now but obviously this won’t be transformative AI because, well, there is no data on transformative AI. 

Then there are macro economists. They work with a set of pretty standard models and mainly expand them by slowly adding/subtracting different sectors or micro founding factors of production in different ways. Many of the arguments are on the parameter values that we should assume when simulating the economy. Early research on transformative AI started there—as demonstrated recently by Chad, Anton et al, the different levels of transformation are due to different assumptions on parameters rather than some new type of economics. The same model can predict basically no impact of AI vs huge transformation, it’s all about assumptions on parameters. 

Finally there is micro theory. This is where decision theory, game theory, mech design, org econ (sort of) live. This field works by setting out a set of assumptions and then *deriving* the expected results; alternatively one could start with a result and work backwards to derive the necessary and sufficient assumptions. There is a ton of potential here to do work on transformative AI: start with assumptions on how AI differs than human agents (eg relax basic assumptions on constraints, on scarcity, introduce completely different objective functions), then derive implications. But this is where there is the least amount of work, and it’s important for that to change (and I believe that it already is). 

I think we can make a ton of progress from these three subfields on better understanding the potential AGI and post AGI transformation. 

But there is another scenario, post strong ASI, where I don’t think economics has much to say about. Here I agree with @Jabaluck that the economy (if you can even call it that) and the agents in it will be so vastly different and beyond our imagination that I wouldn’t know where to start modeling it. Not to discourage others, but post singularity seems like pure epistemic uncertainty to me. 

A lot of the critiques I hear about AI and economics come from people who don’t quite get what economists do. They look around at different results and if they don’t like some of them, they say “oh economics isn’t “pilled” or something. But economists don’t debate results, they *derive* results from assumptions. Thats where the debate is. Saying “but you don’t understand a world with 15 billion  AI agents”. What does that mean for the economy? What are those agents doing, who is buying what they are producing, what do property rights look like? Depending on those assumptions you’ll get vastly different economic scenarios, from 2% growth and high human labor share to completely alien centralized systems with no prices or markets.

text:
My post about Hitler and the far right got millions of views. Clearly, it hit a nerve. So today I'm going to show you, step by step, why the notion of "far right" as it's used in France makes almost no sense. And why the people who wield it are usually the last ones who should be lecturing anyone.

Let's start with the only question that matters: what makes a political system work or fail? To a very large extent, it's the economy. A country that produces wealth, that lets its citizens create, trade and build, stays standing. A country that destroys that collapses, no matter how beautiful its slogans are.

And in economics, there are really only two worldviews.

The first is collectivism. The idea that the State knows better than you. That it must plan production, set prices, run companies, decide what you earn, what you buy, and eventually what you think. The individual is just a cog serving a grand collective project: the class, the nation, the race, the people.

The second is freedom. Capitalism, property, individual liberty, individual responsibility. The idea that millions of people creating value for one another produce infinitely more prosperity than an office of planners, however brilliant they may be.

Now look at the list of the great totalitarian regimes of the 20th century. Stalin: total planning, forced collectivization, millions dead. Mao: the Great Leap Forward and the deadliest famine in human history. Pol Pot: money abolished, cities emptied, nearly a quarter of Cambodia's population exterminated. Mussolini, the man who coined the word fascism: "Everything within the State, nothing outside the State, nothing against the State." And Hitler, leader of the National Socialist German Workers' Party, whose program proclaimed "the common good before individual good." He subjected the entire German economy to State plans: the Four-Year Plan, frozen prices and wages, unions dissolved into a single state labor front, industrialists producing whatever the regime decided.

Their flags were different. Their designated enemies were different. But the machinery was the same: the individual doesn't exist, only the collective matters, and the State decides everything.

Why does it always end in totalitarianism? Because collectivism doesn't work. And when a system doesn't work, it has only two options: admit failure or force people. They always choose force.

Ludwig von Mises proved it as early as 1920: without free prices, without a market, a planner simply cannot know what to produce, how much, or at what cost. He is flying blind. A planned economy isn't a less efficient version of the market. It's an impossibility.

Friedrich Hayek drew the political conclusion in 1944 in The Road to Serfdom, a book he dedicated "to the socialists of all parties." One chapter is titled "The Socialist Roots of Naziism." Another, "Why the Worst Get on Top." For Hayek, controlling the economy isn't controlling one sector among others. It is "the control of the means for all our ends." Whoever controls your bread controls your life. Then your speech. Then your thoughts.

Milton Friedman put it his own way: a society that puts equality before freedom ends up with neither.

So we know exactly what works. It's not an opinion. It's a century of real-world experiments. Listen to the Austrian school, Mises and Hayek, with Friedman from Chicago alongside them: economic freedom, limited government, individual responsibility.

And this is where we get to the great accusatory inversion. Part of the left-wing press spends its time screaming fascism. Why? Because the fascism fantasy is the best way to never talk about the track record of their own ideas. Deep down, they know: if their collectivist program were applied all the way, it wouldn't work, because a collective economy cannot work. And an economy that doesn't work always ends up having to coerce, surveil and ban. In other words, it becomes exactly what they claim to be fighting. The real heirs of totalitarian logic are not the ones being pointed at.

So who gets called "far right" in 2026? People who want safe cities. People who want to keep their culture. People who just want to live a peaceful life, raise their kids, and not have to board up their shop every weekend. People who want the law to apply to everyone.

If that's the far right, then the word no longer means anything. And maybe that was the point.

Polymarket significantly changed the rules for the second time yesterday on the Russia x NATO military clash market, after $7m had already been traded.

The new rules state that interceptions of strikes on ships in NATO countries territorial waters (which is sovereign territory), won’t be considered as a military clash.

The original rules did not have any such carveout and it is impossible to know where Polymarkets bar-raising will finish before we place a bet on these markets. For example, would an intentional drone strike on Bucharest that is intercepted count if the target was a foreign-owned civilian building? Would the US defending a cruise ship from a drone strike while it’s docked in Miami count? (Weirdly, a recon drone shot down over any of those targets would 100% count)

Although I don’t agree with it, I don’t have a huge problem with the actual ruling of the specific incident that was clarified yesterday. I believe the pattern of strikes on nearby ships, alongside statements from President Dan and EU officials, provided strong enough evidence of targeting Romanian territory. But it's a judgment call that could go either way.

The trouble is the bar has now been raised significantly again for future incidents when millions has already been traded, and we can’t accurately price these markets without predictability that rules won’t change under our feet.

text:
The market still prices $NEAR like an L1 that missed its moment. It's 74% below its 2022 high

@Bitwise prices it as the chain AI agents run on, with a $155 base case for 2030. That's about 30x from $5.26

BlackRock's research paper "The Machine-Native Economy" describes the same outlook. Agents that find, buy, and pay for compute on their own

In the paper's words, agents "query real-time marketplace APIs to compare available capacity by price, performance, latency, location, and hardware specialization," then pay "on a per-use, per-model-token, or per-job basis"

NEAR already runs two pieces of that:

1. NEAR Intents: you say what you want and solvers route it across chains. $33.99B in volume to date, $4.84B in the last 30 days (DefiLlama), and its fee share has bought back NEAR since February
2. NEAR AI Cloud: private inference inside secure hardware, now a provider on OpenRouter, and running private sessions in Brave's Leo assistant

When I asked Matt Hougan on @MilkRoadDaily whether Bitwise's call was absurd, he said NEAR could 40x or 50x, and that "doesn't strike me as absurd if it actually executes on this vision"

His framing: Intents alone roughly justifies today's price, and the AI goal comes "like a moonshot for free"

For context, $155 a NEAR works out to about a $200B market cap. That's still below ETH's $298B today

Wall Street is already buying in. Bitwise's spot NEAR ETF launched Sept 29 and took in $35.5M on day one, which Hougan called "a Bitcoin ETF style success"

It's important to say that these price predictions are ambitious, and not necessarily going to play out in NEAR's favor. Ryan Rasmussen said their model assumes "a very high likelihood that this doesn't work out," and the bear case in the report is $1.63

If agents end up buying their own compute, the chain built around that job looks cheap at a $6B market cap

It's a risky bet, but the upside is a huge moonshot.

Full disclosure: $NEAR is a position in my Milk Road PRO portfolio. Our PRO team was early to $UNI (+54.8%), $AERO (+93.7%), and $SOL (+39.1%)

text:
US stock valuations are facing a notable divergence, with September 2026 data showing the S&P 500 trading at a 5-year CAPE of approximately 28.3x, while 10-year real yields are about 62 basis points higher than potential real GDP growth.

-> Real interest rates are putting pressure on valuation ratios, but the stock market is maintaining high P/E ratios, near the levels seen during the peak valuation periods of 2000 and 2021.

Historically, valuation ratios are often high when real yields are slightly lower than potential real growth.

When real yields fall too far below growth, inflation can erode valuation ratios; conversely, when real yields significantly exceed growth, high capital costs often put pressure on P/E ratios to narrow.

The current position is on the side of higher real yields over growth, but CAPE remains near 30x – a mismatch between discounted conditions and market valuations.

Corporate earnings, growth expectations, and the concentration of high-quality businesses could sustain high valuations for longer than anticipated. However, with high CAPE, the market will be more sensitive to changes in real yields and earnings prospects.

text:
GitHub 上有一个恐怖的开源项目，叫 yt-dlp。它没有华丽的界面，没有庞大的人工智能模型，却拿到了近乎整个视频互联网的钥匙。 

YouTube、B 站、TikTok，全球大量视频网站都在它的支持范围内。只需要输入一个链接，它就能自动提取视频、音频、字幕，甚至批量处理整个播放列表。

几小时的视频，一行命令就能开始下载。 但真正令人震撼的，是这个项目和人工智能结合之后会发生什么。

把 yt-dlp 接上 Whisper，再接上 GPT 或 Claude，一套自动化流水线就诞生了。它可以持续收集公开的视频，转录讲话，提取观点，分析信息，自动生成文章。

以前你需要花三个小时看完一场技术发布会，现在人工智能可以在获取内容后迅速提炼出几十条有价值的信息。

这意味着什么？意味着视频正在从只能由人类观看的内容，变成机器能够大规模处理的数据。过去互联网竞争的是谁能吸引更多人的注意力，未来竞争的可能是谁能让人工智能获取、理解更多信息。

更可怕的是，这个项目完全开源，普通人也能使用。一个免费工具，正在成为人工智能理解视频互联网的重要入口。

Moderna与默沙东合作开发的Intismeran，也叫V940／mRNA-4157，会根据每位患者肿瘤的独特突变，定制一份mRNA“识别说明书”，帮助免疫系统发现并攻击癌细胞。

每份药物最多编码34种患者特异性新抗原。

本次研究用于黑色素瘤患者完成手术之后，目标是降低残留癌细胞导致的复发和转移。它与K药配合：疫苗帮助免疫系统识别目标，K药解除限制免疫细胞活动的抑制信号。

🟠 Ⅲ期结果：在现有标准治疗上，增加了多少效果？

INTerpath-001纳入1,137名肿瘤已完整切除、仍有较高复发风险的IIB—IV期患者。

757人接受“疫苗＋K药”，380人接受“安慰剂＋K药”。疫苗最多注射9剂，K药治疗约一年，中位随访24.6个月。

最重要的两个结果：

• 复发或死亡风险降低42%，HR＝0.58。
• 远处转移或死亡风险降低38%，HR＝0.62。

两项结果均达到统计学显著性。

两年无复发生存率为82.2%，对照组70.0%，提高12.2个百分点。对照组本身已经使用有效的K药，因此，这是在现有治疗基础上取得的额外获益。

🟠 会场这页历史对照，说明了突破的难度

此前，在黑色素瘤术后辅助治疗中，多次尝试给PD-1药物再搭配一种免疫药，都未能显著改善无复发生存：

• CheckMate 915：搭配CTLA-4抗体，HR＝0.92。
• RELATIVITY-098：搭配LAG-3抗体，HR＝1.01。
• KEYVIBE-010：搭配TIGIT抗体，HR＝1.25。

这些联合尝试还增加了副作用。

这次个体化疫苗做到HR＝0.58，证明这条技术路线能够在一个此前多次尝试失败的场景里，继续增加疗效。

🟠 哪些患者获益？能否证明活得更久？

不同病期、不同年龄的大多数分组，结果方向支持联合治疗；部分小样本分组仍有较大不确定性。

更关键的是，总体生存数据尚未成熟。

会议报道披露，总体生存HR＝0.77，目前未达到统计学显著性。能否显著延长患者生命，仍需继续随访。

现阶段已经证明减少复发、减少远处转移的获益。82.2%的两年无复发生存率，也不能直接当作治愈率。

🟠 副作用是否明显增加？

3—5级治疗相关不良反应：
• 联合组14.2%，对照组13.4%。

全部原因的3级以上不良反应：
• 联合组23.6%，对照组20.3%。

这两个口径要分别看。

联合组常见反应包括发热52.2%、注射部位疼痛51.0%、疲劳38.5%。公司表示未发现新的安全信号。

据会议报道，治疗相关不良反应导致停用任一研究药物的比例为14.0%，对照组8.7%；联合组有2例治疗相关死亡，均被归因于K药，没有死亡被归因于Intismeran。

🟠 一人定制一份药，生产能否跟上？

Moderna官方确认：进入联合治疗组的患者，疫苗生产成功率超过99%。

会议报道还披露：
• 共筛查1,749人，其中302人因肿瘤样本不足被排除，占17.3%。
• 91%的随机入组患者识别出了可用于设计的34种新抗原。
• 首次接受疫苗的中位时间为64天。

🟠 到底符合预期吗？

市场会前没有统一标准。

公开报道中：
• William Blair把HR不高于0.70视为积极结果。
• UBS曾以0.65作为参考。
• Leerink认为低于0.60会是令人振奋的结果。

实际无复发生存HR＝0.58，达到了这些门槛。

但部分资金期待更接近0.50的强劲效果。RBC提到，一些投资者期待0.50—0.59，0.58落在这一范围获益较弱的一端。

评价是：临床结果扎实，达到了多家机构公开提出的标准；相对更乐观的股价预期，惊喜程度有限。

此前Ⅱ期随访得到的49%与本次Ⅲ期42%，来自不同人群、样本量和随访时间，不能直接得出“疗效退步7个百分点”的结论。

🟠 数据有效，为什么股价还跌？

核心数据10月22日因提前泄露而公开，MRNA当天收跌17.6%。

此前股价已经大幅上涨，部分资金期待的内容还包括：更强的疗效，以及这项技术未来能在多个癌种取得成功。

这次黑色素瘤Ⅲ期，验证了一个重要适应症；肺癌、肾癌、膀胱癌等领域，还需要各自的临床数据。

🟠 对未来股价，如何看待

短期，这份结果降低了黑色素瘤项目的研发风险，对基本面有利；股价仍可能大幅波动。

中期，重点看审批和商业化。公司提到2027年潜在获批，但具体时间仍待监管决定。

另外，按合作协议，Moderna与默沙东的成本和利润原则上各分一半，估值时需要考虑这一点。

长期，更大的上行空间取决于其他癌种能否复制效果。目前INTerpath项目包含9项Ⅱ期、Ⅲ期试验，其中3项正在开展的Ⅲ期针对非小细胞肺癌。

结果评价：黑色素瘤Ⅲ期已经交出一份有分量的答卷。下一阶段，审批进展、真实销售，以及其他癌种的独立验证，会逐步决定它能支撑多大的长期价值。

quoted_text:
About the intismeran presentation at #ESMO26 $MRNA $MRK 

My impression of discussant talk given by Inge Marie Svane of the University of Copenhagen was that she was positive if not overly enthusiastic about INTerpath-001. 

"Measured" might be the best, single adjective. 

"Brutal" is how an investor in the audience described the tone of her talk to me. (He was short Moderna, so there's that.) I disagree.  Brutal is too harsh. If people were expecting Svane to jump for joy, then yes, she did not meet that expectation. To me, she played it mostly straight down the middle. 

She took no position on the mRNA vaccine vs neoadjuvant debate. (Slide below)

She noted the lack of intismerna OS benefit, but said the same about neoadjuvant therapy. She also noted greater toxicity associated with neoadjuvant. 

For intismeran, Svane also raised the question about what exactly was driving the vaccine’s benefit — was it the specific targeting of the neoantigens, or was it the general immune boost that studies have suggested mRNA vaccines generally provide?

Again, we're truly sorry to everyone affected.

text:
Ken Griffin, who runs Citadel, just admitted that the biggest advantage of giant funds, armies of people and billion-dollar budgets, is disappearing

And for the first time in history, a small team with AI can move faster than a hedge fund

He’s seen it in his own firm. His AI agent does in 2-3 hours what used to take Citadel’s PhD researchers 6-8 weeks

A fund runs one cycle: come up with a strategy, turn it into code, test it on history, deploy it to the market

Every step used to cost separate people and years of training. Now AI does the whole cycle

You describe an idea in words, it writes the strategy itself, runs it on years of real data, and if it’s alive, deploys it straight to a broker

But the speed isn’t the point. The point is what the retail trader doesn’t understand

You take a strategy with a beautiful chart and you believe it. But a beautiful chart is no proof

Run enough versions and a profitable curve will appear even on random numbers. One just got lucky, and you decided you found gold

Funds don’t trust any curve until they test it on data the strategy has never seen. There the fit falls apart, and a real edge survives

I ran two of the most-cited quant papers through this cycle

Time Series Momentum on Bitcoin: +1,537%. Alive

Betting Against Beta, a classic from every textbook: minus 7.78% a year while the market rose 14.86%. A corpse

One still prints money, the other died long ago. And trading blind, you’d never know which is which until it took your deposit

Griffin says the future belongs to small teams with AI. But the only ones who win are the ones who test before they bet

How to plug your AI into real market data so it runs this exact test instead of guessing, in the article below

体脂率、肌肉量、尤其骨密度的临床标准（图4）。
是高端家用8电极体脂秤、Inbody也无法代替的。

今年1月我发了下方引用推，关于
“骨骼健康重要，但被普遍低估的底层逻辑”。
当时做了一次DEXA检测，
对下肢的骨密度不太满意。

后来因为卧推受伤，
所以我3月开始打网球，至今半年，周均3小时，
减少约2/3的上肢无氧训练。

昨天10月4日我再检测，骨骼改善效果相当明显：
髋部股骨骨密度 +6.4% （图1）；
年龄增加，但全身骨密度不仅没流失，还小幅增加；
内脏脂肪 398g➡️355g，-10.8%

相当于这半年，我用自己身体实验，
完全验证了⬇️引用推里，
关于优化骨骼方法的第5~7层理论。

下半身的骨骼质量
≈
下半生的腿脚好不好，还能不能活蹦乱跳

这么长期一举多得的事情，得保持做。
接下来要再接再厉，把网球常年打下去，

We owe you an apology.

On October 20, we detected unauthorized access to our official website. After verifying API activity with Shopify, we confirmed on October 23 that a third party obtained customer shipping information. You trusted us with those details, and we're sorry we didn't keep them safe.

Exposed: names, contact details, shipping addresses, and order details (items and prices).
Not exposed: payment card or bank details, recovery phrases, private keys, or wallet passwords.

We've blocked access, fixed the vulnerability, opened an investigation, and are emailing affected customers.

Scammers may pose as Keystone by phone, text, email, or mail, offering refunds, replacement devices, or "fixes" for your order or address. None of it is from us.

NEVER share your recovery phrase or private keys, and NEVER enter your recovery phrase into a device you didn't order. We will never ask for them. Don't click links in unexpected messages. Type https://t.co/7km8AZM288 yourself.

A detailed report is coming soon.

Until then, trust only our official channels. If anything feels off, email support@keyst.one. We'd rather hear from you than have you take a chance.

Again, we're truly sorry to everyone affected.

text:
The internet is coming out of LOCKDOWN.

“Black October” has seen MILLIONS of hacking attempts as two critical PHP flaws triggered emergency shutdowns across governments, banks and major platforms.

If these headlines have left you worried, there’s another part of the story you need to see.

As of October 23, no government or security firm had confirmed a single successful PHP2Shell attack.

Websites that went dark are coming back.

Wikipedia had outages during the scramble and was back up the next day.

US banks have dodged early damage too, per American Banker.

Here’s how the world is fighting BACK:

Cloudflare switched on protection hours before the official fix came out, even for free users.

PHP shipped fixes for both flaws on October 21, a day after details leaked.

Big hosts and clouds like Hostinger, Google and Amazon rolled out updates to the PHP they manage for customers.

Governments told site owners to patch or go offline.

Many shutdowns were deliberate precautions, giving operators time to install those fixes.

Getting the fixes onto every affected system is now the challenge.

Anyone managing a PHP server needs to confirm the fixes are installed.

A third, separate PHP issue disclosed on October 23 has a temporary workaround while its software fix is prepared.

That issue requires an unusual combination of settings and application behavior.

There is still no reliable worldwide count of websites that have finished patching.

Security firm NCC Group warns there’s “a real possibility” some vulnerable systems were already compromised.

For us, there are precautions worth taking now.

Secure your email with a unique password and enable passkeys or 2FA.

Replace any passwords you’ve reused across accounts.

Check official notices from services you use.

Check unexpected account warnings by opening the official app or website directly.

Keep your devices updated through official settings.

Never install a supposed “PHP patch” sent in a message.

Run a website? Check with your host that PHP itself is patched, since WordPress and plugins run on top of PHP and can’t fix it.

We don’t yet know what the coming months or ongoing investigations will reveal.

But fixes are being deployed, defenses are being strengthened and there are steps we can take today.

We can’t prevent every company breach, but we can make it harder for one breach to spread into the rest of our lives.
author: crypto_bitlord7
quoted_text:
The internet is going into a LOCKDOWN.

Hundreds of millions of websites are potentially at risk from cyberattacks.

Governments, banks and major platforms have already taken their websites OFFLINE.

Many are already calling it “Black October.”

At the centre of the shutdowns is something most of us have never heard of, but use every day.

PHP, the software behind roughly 7 in 10 websites, has two critical flaws that can let hackers break in without a password.

Dubbed PHP2Shell, both are rated 9.2 out of 10 for severity.

Details began circulating on Oct 20. Emergency fixes arrived the next day, but attackers were already moving.

Cloudflare’s CEO says hacking attempts then jumped from thousands to MILLIONS within hours.

Cybersecurity agencies across several countries are telling PHP site owners the same thing: Patch it now, or take it offline.

Websites have gone dark worldwide, from government portals and hospitals to banks.

CrowdStrike warns these attacks leave almost no trace, so some sites may not know if they’ve been hit.

Around 2.6 MILLION internet-facing servers run PHP, potentially hosting hundreds of sites each.

Over 1.1 million use older versions no longer receiving official PHP updates.

Older installations may need an upgrade to a supported PHP version or a fix from their software provider.

And patching does not remove a backdoor an attacker may already have planted.

Cloudflare also says hackers are now tweaking their attacks to try to slip past its protections.

But PHP isn’t the only security story unfolding.

-Japan’s Onamae suspended ALL Desktop Cloud plans after malware was found on customer servers.

-India’s eMudhra had 8 website-certificate keys so weak, one was literally the number “4”.

-State Bank of India confirmed 3,897 customer records on the dark web.

-Criminals used AI agents to break into 400+ Latin American banks.

-Capcom confirmed a breach exposing 11.7 million email addresses.

-GitLab disclosed a 10/10 severity flaw in versions going back to 2014.

-LiteLLM removed a malware-containing release. Railway reported possible exposure of customer secrets.

None of these has a confirmed link to PHP2Shell.

We’re seeing separate breaches unfold together.

The true number of incidents could take months to come out.

The world is still on alert. Attacks are still coming.

One year in at @katana . It's been a ride.

This past year has been one of the most intense and rewarding periods of growth for me, both on the business side and as a developer.

What started as a Developer Relations role evolved into so much more. I've had the opportunity to contribute across product, marketing, AI optimization, community, engineering, and feature design.

But the dev in me never stopped getting my hands dirty on the technical side.

I've built and operated liquidation bots, perps trading bots, AI-driven delta-neutral strategy bots, and arbitrage bots (still haven't figured out how to make that arbitrage profitable, lmao).

One of the biggest takeaways, though, has been the people I've worked alongside.

We're a tight team and I've learned something from every single person.

The Katana Perps team are true OGs. Watching their meticulous approach to engineering, optimization, and execution has been an education in itself. When a team has worked together for over seven years, you can see it in how they operate, solve problems, and build. That kind of chemistry is hard to replicate.

It's been intense. My socials haven't been nearly as active as they used to be, but that's because I've been heads down, building, experimenting, learning, and constantly pushing myself to improve.

One year in, and I still feel like there's so much more to learn and build.

text:
马斯克说：“未来金钱将失去意义。”
奥特曼反手一刀：“埃隆想多了，10年后钱依然重要得很。”

奥特曼的意思其实很露骨：
1 物质通缩？同意。 AI确实会让商品、服务和算力成本雪崩。

2 消灭金钱？扯淡。 成本跌了不等于免费，更不等于大家都能躺平。

3 核心恐慌是“阶级固化”： 奥特曼直言，AI最危险的不是产生意识，而是技术与资本极度集中在极少数人手里。AI不会自动消灭贫富差距，只会像杠杆一样把它撬得更夸张。

4 至于人类会不会被灭？ 奥特曼秒答：“概率极低。”

埃隆聊的是50年后的终极幻想，奥特曼算的是未来10年的资产负债表。

现实是：生产要素可能归零，但稀缺性永远存在。未来拉开人与人之间差距的，不再是勤奋，而是你究竟是在消费AI，还是在用AI构建资产。

你站马斯克的乌托邦，还是奥特曼的现实主义？

On 22nd October, Holy Mother Church celebrates Pope Saint John Paul II’s optional Memorial, which marks his installation Mass to the Papacy on 22 October 1978.

In his first homily of his papacy, he aptly captured the cultural despair of a post-Christian world, and pointed to the antidote: 

“So often today man does not know what is within him, in the depths of his mind and heart. So often he is uncertain about the meaning of his life on this earth. He is assailed by doubt, a doubt which turns into despair. We ask you therefore, we beg you with humility and trust, let Christ speak to man. He alone has words of life, yes, of eternal life.”

Throughout his life, John Paul II fought back against a world broken by fear and despair. His life and legacy exist as a great refutation of Satan’s lies and fear mongering. Notably however, he did not dwell frequently on the enemy in his words, though he was always aware of the threat. Instead, with unwavering faith in the Resurrection, he lived his life in tremendous joy, even through his long years of suffering and illness.

John Paul II encourages us to, like the first disciples, follow Jesus! To not be afraid to draw near to Him, to cross the threshold of His dwelling, to speak with Him, face to face, as you talk with a friend (cf. Ex 33:11). To not be afraid of the “new life” He is offering. He Himself makes it possible

text:
Three arms, one island

The Celts swore their oaths by three things: unless the sky falls, unless the sea breaks its bounds, unless the earth opens beneath us. Three realms, held together by a promise.

Their sign for it turns: the triskele, three arms spinning from one centre. On the Isle of Man it is still the flag, and legend says it is the sea god Manannán himself, rolling across the mist on three legs. An island in the middle of the sea, wearing three arms.

And their Otherworld was always an island across the water. The Isle of Apples. The Land of Youth. Hy-Brasil, seen once in seven years. The kingdom under the wave. Ys, Lyonesse, the drowned lands their bards would not forget.

Inside Newgrange, older than any Celt, the triple spiral is cut in the dark. The Celts inherited it and made the mound a home of gods.

In Ethiopia that sign is a landscape.

The upper water: the springs and lakes of the highland plateau, 2,500 metres up, where the river is born. The heavens’ water, falling and gathered.

The middle water: the Awash, descending through its valley, twelve stations from the plateau to the plain. The living river, the water that walks.

The lower water: the salt. The depression sinks below the level of the sea, and there the river never reaches the ocean. It dies into the terminal lakes, into brine, into the underworld laid bare.

Three waters, three worlds, stacked one above the other in rock and air. And where do they meet?

At one point only: the island in the terminal lake, where the waters of the plateau arrive by the river and stand still above the salt.

The centre the three arms turn around, a centre that held everything around it. The triskelion is the same idea drawn in one line: three worlds, one hub.

#Atlantis #CelticMythology #Triskelion

text:
*Post 1/12*  
I CANCELLED MY FUNERAL™  
CHAPTER 2: BARN, BLOOD, STARS  
by Ulyssesfve2™  

I came out of the barn dirty with blood 4:50am. Knife still in my hand. The air was cold, and the only sound was my own breathing and the drip of something I didn’t want to look at.  
I didn’t wipe it off. Didn’t care.  
I looked up at the stars and pointed the knife right at them.  
“Nothing’s gonna stop humanity from taking you,” I said. Stupid? Maybe 

*Post 2/12*  
I pointed that knife at the stars and made the promise like it was a contract.  
“Nothing’s gonna stop humanity from getting up there.”  
And I meant it.  
Not because I’d read it somewhere.  
I meant it because I was standing there, blood on my hands, pocket heavy with money I actually earned.  
From nothing.  
Building housing, climbing out of nowhere, sleeping in places you wouldn’t park a car.

*Post 3/12*  
If a guy like me could make it that far, then what’s stopping the rest of us?  
I felt it in my chest — the invisibility of the human spirit.  
How it bends but doesn’t break.  
My pocket was heavy. Coins and notes stuffed in the inside of my jacket, pressing against my ribs.  
Cash in hand, no bank, no mortgage, no 25 years of interest eating you alive.

*Post 4/12*  
Right in front of me was Baldur.  
The finest bull this area ever produced.  
He ran at me from the fields the way he always did, expecting feed, expecting me.  
I had to slaughter him.  
It’s not clean. The knife has to find the exact spot, and you have to commit. The blood came hot, fast, and it soaked into the dirt, into my boots.

*Post 5/12*  
There’s a smell to it — iron and earth and something primal that sticks in your nose for days.  
Money in the pocket, blood on the hands.And the worst part? It made sense.I was there when Baldur was born.
*3 AM*, freezing, cow on her side bawling, and me with my arm elbow-deep trying to turn him right so he wouldn’t die.

*Post 6/12*  
For the next 2 years I fed him, checked him, knew his limp before the vet did.  You name them even when you tell yourself not to.  
You talk to them when it’s 2 AM and you can’t sleep.But you’re not supposed to love livestock. That’s rule one. Love gets in the way of the ledger.

*Post 7/12*  
And then the clients start queuing up.  Not people. Hyenas. Smiling, “When’s it ready? How much for the cut? Supermarket is cheaper.” I’m collecting the money, counting it, feeling the notes stick together with sweat.And every note feels like 30 pieces of silver.

*Post 8/12*  
Because I’m the one who raised him.  I’m the one he ran to.  
And I’m the one turning that trust into cash.  By the gate.  
Seven guys who’d followed me through winters with no heating, summers where we slept in half-built houses.  They didn’t say anything when they saw me.  
Blood on my jacket, knife still in my hand, Baldur’s body behind me steaming in the cold.

*Post 9/12*  
They knew.  Generosity makes people uncomfortable when they’re the ones benefiting.  
Give a man a bonus when he expects minimum wage, and for 10 seconds he’s grateful.  After that, he starts wondering what you want from him.  But they still would’ve followed me to hell.  Because I’d bled with them.

*Post 10/12*  
The crew was quiet because they were already doing the math.  
About me.  When you stand there with cash in your pocket and a dead animal at your feet, people stop seeing a man.  They see a resource.  A faucet.  A threat.

*Post 11/12*  
The guy who’d carry you out of a fire yesterday is now wondering if you’ll cut his pay tomorrow.

text:
What can we remove?

Our bias is to always add more. More rules, more procedures, more code, more features, more stuff. Interdependencies proliferate, and gradually strangle us. Systems want to grow and grow, but without pruning, they collapse. Slowly, then spectacularly.

When a piece of trash drifts across the beach, it is our duty to pick it up so the next person can enjoy a pristine shoreline. When a thousand pieces litter the beach, it is too late. We can only lament the landscape. That’s just how beaches are now.

A good system is designed to be periodically cleared of cruft. It has a built-in counterbalance. Without this pressure, our bias drives us to add band-aid after band-aid, until the only choice is to destroy the whole system and start from scratch.

Why is it so much easier to add than to remove? Maybe because we attach our identity to what is visible. But there is a difference between the ornamentation that defines our style and the vestigial burdens we carry.

Remember those who did the invisible work of removing. Their legacy was not to build a sand castle, but to care for the beautiful beach on which we play.

author: visavishesh
quoted_text:
The only way out is through. 

They're calling it the Bugpocalypse. LLMs are being used to find long-hidden cracks in the software infrastructure, and it's happening at a furious rate. 3% of all compromises in computing history happened in the last week, claims one source? I believe it.

There are people saying public access to the frontier models ought to be locked out, or heavily guardrailed, over this. The problem with that idea can be summed up in one sentence: when lockpicks are outlawed, only outlaws will have lockpicks.

The lockpicks will be Chinese open-weight models, if nothing else. There's no way to stop those from becoming ubiquitous.

There are two futures in front of us. One in which only the bad guys have lockpicks, and security holes go undiscovered until they're exploited. Another in which everybody has lockpicks and is aggressively red-teaming their own software so it gets fixed before the holes are exploited. 

The corpus of human code is huge but finite. The number of defects in it has to be finite too. We can fix those defects now; we have a million friendly robots to do it with.

The only way out is through.

text:
我有一个大胆的预测：

AI逆向工程的成熟，可能让游戏行业迎来新一轮私服浪潮，而Web3的GameFi模式，或许会成为传统游戏厂商被迫寻找的最后一片净土。

很多人可能不知道，陈志早年就与私服产业有着密切关联。

过去，架设一款网游私服需要相当高的技术门槛：逆向工程、协议破解、服务端重构、数据库还原，以及后续的运维。

但AI正在迅速压低这些成本。

当AI Agent能够自主分析客户端、重构服务器逻辑、复现游戏机制，甚至持续生成游戏内容时，传统游戏厂商依赖技术壁垒建立的垄断将面临前所未有的挑战。

以前破解一款游戏需要一个技术团队，未来可能只需要一个人和一群AI Agent。

这意味着什么？

游戏的复制成本将趋近于零，而传统游戏的商业模式却高度依赖人为制造的稀缺性。

装备、金币、角色、等级、皮肤，乃至整个游戏世界，本质上都是中心化服务器数据库中的一串数字。

当任何人都能低成本复制一套游戏世界，厂商又该如何证明这些数字的价值？

我认为，这可能成为GameFi真正的历史性机会。

过去Web3游戏总想着用Token吸引玩家，用Play to Earn挑战传统游戏，结果往往陷入庞氏经济与死亡螺旋。

但下一轮GameFi的逻辑可能完全不同。

当游戏内容不再稀缺，真正稀缺的将是不可随意复制的经济共识、资产所有权和玩家网络。

游戏可以被复制，代码可以被Fork，服务器可以被重建。

但一个拥有真实玩家、持续交易、流动性与长期经济关系的生态，很难仅靠复制代码就完整迁移。

这恰恰是区块链能够提供差异化价值的地方。

未来游戏厂商可能不得不放弃对虚拟世界的绝对控制权，通过链上资产、开放经济系统和可验证的所有权，把玩家从消费者转变为生态利益相关者。

当然，区块链无法阻止游戏被复制，也无法凭空创造稀缺性。

但它可以让游戏的价值逐渐脱离单一服务器和运营商，沉淀在玩家共同认可的经济网络之中。

AI负责无限生产游戏世界，区块链负责有限确权与价值结算。

一个解决供给，一个解决产权。

这可能才是AI × GameFi真正值得关注的方向。

回顾互联网的发展史，很多颠覆性创新都来自旧秩序的防御性反击。

当技术壁垒被AI击穿，传统游戏厂商可能会发现，过去最不愿意放弃的中心化控制权，反而成为未来最大的负担。

技术进步最残酷的地方，在于它会不断消灭旧时代赖以收费的稀缺性。

当复制成为常态，价值就必须寻找新的锚。

也许Web3游戏真正的爆发，从来不需要一场主动的革命。

只需要AI把传统游戏厂商逼到墙角。

这就是倒逼式创新。

text:
The only way out is through. 

They're calling it the Bugpocalypse. LLMs are being used to find long-hidden cracks in the software infrastructure, and it's happening at a furious rate. 3% of all compromises in computing history happened in the last week, claims one source? I believe it.

There are people saying public access to the frontier models ought to be locked out, or heavily guardrailed, over this. The problem with that idea can be summed up in one sentence: when lockpicks are outlawed, only outlaws will have lockpicks.

The lockpicks will be Chinese open-weight models, if nothing else. There's no way to stop those from becoming ubiquitous.

There are two futures in front of us. One in which only the bad guys have lockpicks, and security holes go undiscovered until they're exploited. Another in which everybody has lockpicks and is aggressively red-teaming their own software so it gets fixed before the holes are exploited. 

The corpus of human code is huge but finite. The number of defects in it has to be finite too. We can fix those defects now; we have a million friendly robots to do it with.

The only way out is through.

text:
Interestingly, Apple Silicon also has the same basic multi-die structure as Nvidia Blackwell.

Most high-end local devices now do some version of this: multiple physical dies fused into one logical chip so software sees a single unified processor with shared memory. 

Apple M5 series is a good example of this.

Base M5 is a conventional single-die SoC. 10 CPU cores and 10 GPU cores.

M5 Pro is where multi-die starts. Apple calls it the Fusion Architecture. It combines two heterogeneous dies into one SoC. One primarily for the CPU, Neural Engine, and I/O, the other for the GPU and memory controller. The CPU die now supports 18 cores and GPU die to 20 cores.

M5 Max keeps the exact same CPU configuration and dual-die Fusion layout as the Pro, but doubles the GPU cores (and the associated memory bandwidth) to 40 cores. 

M5 Ultra takes it further. Two of those M5 Max chips are packaged and fused together with UltraFusion. This is where both sides doubles: the CPU cores go from 18 to 36 and the GPU cores from 40 to 80. The result is a quad-die chip that still presents as one unified processor to software, with the inter-die link running at over 4.4 TB/s.

DGX Spark and AMD Halo also connect multiple dies inside a single package. Their inter-die links, though, run at significantly lower bandwidth than Apple’s Fusion and UltraFusion interconnects. Spark is at 600GB/s and Halo is at ~64GB/s.

It’ll be interesting to see when software on Apple improves enough to take more advantage of these physical innovations.
author: 0xkydo
quoted_text:
A fun realization I had recently: with Blackwell (B200 and B300), we are basically back to solving classic NUMA problems inside a single GPU package.

To software, a B200 looks like one big unified GPU. But physically it is two silicon dies connected by NV-HBI. And while that cross-die link is fast, local HBM is still noticeably closer. If you ignore this, memory-heavy workloads like MoE layers spend half their time pulling weights across the link, which burns latency and power for no good reason.

Pay attention to MegaMoE in DeepGEMM. In fact, CUDA doesn’t have an API to tell you which SM sits on which die, so just measure it directly with a few lines of pointer chasing.

1. Slice the weights in half onto physical memory for each die, and run a persistent scheduler where SMs pull from their local die first. 
2. Only steal work across dies if there are at least two full waves of tasks left. Why? 

Otherwise, paying the transit latency for small leftovers just isn't worth it. Then, 4D TMA descriptor can do coordinate routing so the inner loop stays completely clean.

The payoff is ~100 W of package power saved and 5-10% higher sustained clocks. (Which can be hundreds of thousands of $$ saved in real deployment).

text:
Since people are yelling at threat intelligence professional for "downplaying the severity of the PHP vulnerability" (communicating clear concise information about what they're actually seeing). It feels necessary to explain what threat intelligence actually is.

Consider a hypothetical hospital or a power company. A lot of systems are built using very old PHP versions. It's not uncommon for PHP to add/remove/change features from version to version. So if you're a certain number of versions behind, updating to the latest version will break your software by removing or changing functionality it needs.

In that case, the provider has two options: 
1) take their software offline until they can update the code to match the latest PHP version.
2) panic install the patch and break their software, leading to a massive outage.

In both cases, that is basically a 100% chance of an outage. On the other hand, maybe they get hacked, maybe they don't. Maybe that hack causes an outage, maybe it doesn't. Realistically, under these circumstances, the chance of an outage is actually higher with patching than with not patching.

If that outage would result in the hospital having to shut its doors or a power company's infrastructure going offline, what is the correct move? Chance being hacked, or knowingly cause an outage that threatens lives?

Cybersecurity is important and all, but there are risks far greater than being hacked. I would absolutely love it if I could just log onto IDontKnowWhyTheyRenamedThisSite dot Com, be like "vulnerability bad, pls patch" and everyone installs the patch. That is not the world we live in. 

Now, if I start seeing people building ransomware that can copy itself from system to system using the PHP vulnerability, and I communicate that, it changes a lot of people's risk calculations. Their option shift towards either a 100% chance of an outage, or an extremely high chance of an outage + catastrophic data loss. In this case they would most likely pull the trigger on patching or taking their software offline.

While the hypotheticals I gave are extreme cases, many organizations accept being hacked as a cost of doing business. Taking offline software that's critical to organizational function is not an easy decision to make, and does not get taken lightly.

We don't live in LaLa land where every org installs every patch for every vulnerability the day it goes live. Cybersecurity is expensive and time consuming. Getting people to even patch systems at all is an endless uphill battle.

Most orgs know that something like 1 out of ever 10,000 critical vulnerabilities actually gets exploited. And probably less than 50% of these "this is the worst of the worst vulnerability ever, the sky is falling" type vulnerabilities leads to significant damages.

It takes a lot of time to build trust, and very little time to lose it. Overhype a couple of vulnerabilities and people will very quickly stop listening to you. It's extremely easy to end up being the boy who cried wolf. There's only so many times you can spin security teams into a frenzy before they stop listening to you entirely.

Orgs also have limited resources, so when you yell fire, there is a good chance they're committing resources they don't have. Making people stay up all night, pulling people off other issues, bringing in outside help. You probably don't want to be responsible for some org getting ransomwared because they redirected all their security resources to some vulnerability you think is really cool.

Nobody is downplaying anything. They are communicating exactly what they see/know about the issue so that organizations can make the most informed risk management decisions possible. That is the game, and that is what threat intelligence exists for.

If you want to handle an organization's security for them and personally take on the risk of potentially costing them billions or killing their customers, join an MSSP or a critical infrastructure provider. I can promise you it's way more stressful than you think.

It's not our job to decide organization's own risk models for them. It's our job to give the most information possible to the people who do. And just because some vulnerability researcher thinks we're not hyping up the vulnerability enough doesn't make them right.

Last I checked, only something like 9.3 million out of 42 million systems had installed the patch. This is the reality we live in. If we yell fire, then maybe we can bump that number up to 10 million, but if nothing happens, it'll be at the cost of maybe 2 million less systems getting patched next time around. 

These are real risks we have to live with. These aren't one-off incidents. People will remember how accurate our advice was the next time around. And more or less people may decide to install security fixes based on how accurately we communicated the risks during previous incidents.

Threat intelligence is an extremely complex numbers game where there is never any right answer.

Canton’s sub-transaction privacy gives each party only its own slice of a transaction, made of three permissions, stakeholder visibility, divulgence, and disclosure.

@Hackenclub has put together examples showing how keeping them distinct decides which party can act on what.
author: CantonNetwork
quoted_text:
On @CantonNetwork, "who can see this contract?" sounds simple. It is actually three questions: who was told about it, who saw it and who is permitted to use it.

Get the distinction wrong and your KYC provider could see the loan rate.

Hacken's new research works through a loan example:
• A KYC provider added as an observer on the loan sees every field, including the amount, rate and lender.
• If the identity moves to a separate contract but is fetched inside the loan's Accept choice, every witness of Accept sees it.
• A better approach is to fetch only a pass/fail attestation rather than the full identity record.

To remove an observer, the contract must be archived and recreated, because Daml contracts are immutable.

The Ledger API is not the boundary. Divulged copies remain in participant storage until pruning, and the receiving party's validator operator can read them.

None of this shows up as a failing test.

Full analysis, with a five-point Daml privacy audit checklist: https://t.co/GmVsWigTSD

author: degennQuant
quoted_text:
Pearl energy usage vs Bitcoin and Zcash both over the last year and since issuance. 

Trend is strong, but it's too early to draw conclusions about Pearl's long term security from this wattage. 

Over time I expect GPU owners to become addicted to Pearl mining rewards, eventually seeing a GPU as the same type of capital investment as an ASIC is today for a Bitcoin or Zcash miner. 

If that happens it would be foolish to use GPUs to attack Pearl, since ruining the network would also ruin some of their CapEx value. 

IMO if Pearl can build a moat on duplex GPU mining and capture a significant share of data center electricity it will be the most secure PoW network (defined as cost to attack). 

Rough math on attack cost is electricity, forgone mining revenue, and a 20-30% depreciation on any GPUs used for the attack. 

Thresholds to watch are the Pearl fp8 transition and continued growth of wattage.

text:
ENA is down 35% from its local high. 

UNI is down 33%. 

And ETH is down 15%. 

All of these have been in a 9-month bear market. All are near oversold on the RSI. All are well below their prior-cycle highs. 

I will never understand the mind of a short-term trader who is long-term bullish.

Why not just buy stuff at or near the bear-market lows? Have a view? And hold through the volatility/stack more? 

The # of things you have to get right and the amount of mental anguish of constantly entering, exiting, rotating, and re-entering introduce so many risk factors that you avoid by simply having a view and being patient, in my opinion. 

I guess that's why I always say investing is *personal.* 

The best investors tend to find what works for them. 

I'm glad I know this strategy will never work for me.

text:
BTC vs ORE: A Comparison of Durability 
__
 
Bitcoin is called Digital Gold but Gold does not need to be kept alive. 

If you bury a gold bar in the dirt for 2,000 years it requires zero electricity, zero maintenance, and zero human attention.  It just exists, surviving passively, not decaying for generations.  
 
Bitcoin does not work that way.  It must consume billions of dollars of electricity every year just to keep its history from being rewritten.  
 
When the last BTC is mined, block rewards disappear, leaving transaction fees to secure and sustain its ledger.  IF those fees don’t materialize, the network starves, security drops, and the asset perishes.  
 
Bitcoin has an expiration risk.  
 
$ORE changes the paradigm entirely.  
 
If everyone stops mining $ORE today, the tokens already in circulation simply sit there on Solana.   They don't require continuous mining to remain recorded on Solana.  

Because $ORE sits on top of Solana, it doesn’t have to maintain and fund a separate L1 network.  Solana pays for its own survival through its massive ecosystem utility and fees.  

So $ORE, like physical gold, can just exist as an immutable element on Solana surviving passively, without decaying. 
 
And there’s more.  

Through $ORE’s buyback & “rebury” loop, $ORE captures capital from economic mining activity, buys tokens off the open market and recycles them back into the system, within the 3 million supply cap.  

So $ORE on Solana not only preserves the asset, it preserves the opportunity for future generations to participate in mining. 
 
Comparatively, $ORE’s SoV properties are structurally closer to Gold than Bitcoin.  
 
- Scarcity that endures.  
- Participation that continues.  
- A digital asset/SoV that doesn’t have to keep being mined to exist. 
 
$ORE – The SoV of SoV’s

NEW: I sat down w/ former Twitter CEO & CTO Parag Agrawal (@paraga)

Now Founder & CEO of $2B Parallel Web Systems (@p0).

Parag says we're underestimating AI agents by 5,000–10,000x, transforming the internet's economics entirely.

Forget the startup benchmark of 3x, 3x, 2x, 2x. Parag benchmarks this new agentic era against the growth of inference, roughly 10x a year, & says every estimate he’s made in this market has come in too low.

Parallel has raised $230M in total funding from funds like @IndexVentures, Kleiner Perkins & Khosla Ventures, building AI-native search infrastructure for customers like: Harvey, Lovable, Granola, Replit, LangChain, Profound, Modal, Notion & Browserbase.

Today, agent web usage is estimated at just 10–20% of human usage. Parag's own agents already run several thousand searches a day, & he believes we're still in the earliest stages of this transition.

The infrastructure implications are massive. Parag predicts that for every 10 GPUs used in model inference, another 1–2 will be required for web search alone.

The economic implications are equally significant. Traditional advertising, subscriptions & affiliate models depend on human attention and browsing behavior. As agents become the primary consumers of information, these models will need to be rebuilt, including how publishers get compensated when agents access their content.

We also covered:
› Why the web is shifting from reactive to proactive AI agents
› Sourcing GPUs & scaling search infrastructure
› Voice agents, latency & token efficiency
› Agent identity, bot detection & cybersecurity
› Scaling Parallel from 30 to 120 employees this year

We also spent time on Parag's 11 years at Twitter, where he went from engineer to CTO to CEO. We discussed the lessons from leading one of the world's most influential social platforms.

text:
turns out robinhood was not paradise

this isn't meant to be a gravedance. for the sake of onchain, i really do hope these coins recover

but im moreso making fun of anyone who claimed robinhood was immune to the same problems that have plagued every other chain/memecoin

multiwalleting, bundling, christmas tree chart patterns, and farmers exist on both solana and robinhood. when the participants are always the same, these problems don't disappear when you bridge to a new chain

the reason robinhood performed so well was because it was the newest and shiniest thing onchain for people to speculate on after bitcoin candled 30% during august-september

despite coins having bad holder distribution initially and/or being bundled, they still performed well because of the sheer amount of volume + people were extremely risk-on

($index is a good example of this ^ team was pillaging the chart through every catalyst but it still went 70m)

yes, in some ways robinhood was objectively better than sol ($meme narrative > anything we've recently seen on sol, also only possible on RH). but this doesn't mean the same problems i mentioned before don't exist across all chains

i still dont think stock pairs are super innovative, but the narrative was fresh enough to send multiple coins to 9 fig mc this last onchain wave

(funnily enough, $cashcat has the "strongest" chart now despite being the most pure memecoin)

the issue onchain is experiencing right now has nothing to do with a specific launchpad, team, exchange, or chain

the truth is onchain just needs to mature, the same way alts have recently matured from random slop outperforming BTC to now only quality alts consistently outperforming ($hype $zec: revenue meta/perps/privacy/sov)

i'm not sure what it will be, but we need something new that's genuinely very innovative or else we will forever be stuck in this cycle

Today, we're announcing that Sundial has been acquired by @Meta! 

Chandra Narayanan and I are joining along with some other incredible members of our team. 

Nearly six years ago, Chandra and I started Sundial with two core beliefs: 1) better decisions come from using data well, and 2) great things come from working on hard problems with people you like.

Sundial automated away many of the obstacles involved in getting to meaningful analysis (Cleaning data! Creating semantic layers! Writing SQL! Storytelling!), and we were proud to support some of the fastest-growing AI companies from OpenAI to Gamma.

We started before the AI wave and rebuilt ourselves to be AI-native. We raised our first round when interest rates were near zero, and our Series A when they were the highest in two decades. We watched customers hyperscale and then close shop, new grads grow into leaders, and software development change completely. 

Entrepreneurship has been my dream since college, when I first took a class on start-ups (shoutout Mayfield Fellows!). I wish I'd been brave enough sooner because there’s no better way to learn how the world works and who you really are than betting on yourself to launch a business.

Meta is my former home and where I learned product and design. It's also one of the most analytically rigorous places on the planet. So many of Sundial's values came from there: questioning assumptions, diagnosing with data, owning the user’s experience. I'm thrilled to bring what we've learned to the place where it all started and continue our mission of improving the quality and velocity of business decisions with people we like.

author: rileybrown
quoted_text:
My unfiltered thoughts on personal agents.

Grokbot has the best UI and it’s arguably the best overall. In a lot of ways they’re ahead. Their desktop app feels the best, and their multi-bot coordination is great: you can set a team lead and it passes tasks to the other bots. Grokbot also has the best “webhook” feature, which means you can easily turn outside events into triggers that start your agents. That speeds up background workflows like watching your email, Slack and more. It also has Cursor integration, so for bigger tasks Grokbot can spin up a Cursor cloud session with any model (until OpenAI cuts SpaceX off from their models, which I think will happen soon). Unfortunately, running frontier models through Cursor costs more than Claude or Codex. Still, they’re the only ones embracing a team of agents. It’s a really cool idea, but the more bots you have, the more time you spend managing and maintaining them. I’m starting to think one bot with different threads/channels is the right answer, which I’ll get to with Claude Duet.

dots by OpenAI is rough around the edges right now, but it’s probably the most powerful if you use Codex, which I do. dots can spin up Codex sessions in the cloud or locally on your computer. So if you have coding or video editing workflows that need your local files, this is very useful. Codex computer use is also the best in the world: your dot can spin up a local Codex session that fully controls your computer, as long as it’s on. Their real-time voice is incredible. If you have your email and work tools connected, try this: go on a walk with headphones in, ask the agent to summarize your emails, have it draft replies and read them back to you, then send them off. If I remember right, this is close to a workflow you (Tim) used to have with your VAs before AI. It’s my favorite use case for personal agents. The one downside is that you have to call your agent, and it’s an awful experience. It literally rings, and it’s annoying.

Muse by Meta is a toy. I’ve talked to a bunch of finance people I play poker with who all tried it and set up automations, and they all said it doesn’t reliably do what they want. It’s fast, and its user numbers will probably keep growing. But it’s basically free: you get a TON of usage without paying a dime. That’s NOT a trade I’m willing to make. An agent doing high-leverage tasks should be running at the Opus 5.5 or GPT 6.1 Sol level.

Claude Duet - is in early access, so unfortunately not everyone can use it yet. First things first, it runs on Opus 5.5, the best model in the world. I’ve only had access for 72 hours, but Duet feels different from the others. It’s not a personified agent like Grokbot, dot or Muse, which gives it a more professional vibe that I like. When you ask your Duet agent to do something, it spins up a task, which is a new chat thread. All your threads show up in a Tasks tab, so it’s easy to see everything Duet is working on or has finished. And instead of creating more agents (like Grokbot), you create channels, just like Slack (I can tell @anthropic is Slack-pilled). I have a content channel, a finances channel, etc., which keeps different kinds of tasks separate. The only other app I’ve seen do this is Buzz by @jack, and it’s a good experience. Their strong point is documents (artifacts). If you want decks, high-quality docs or design mockups, Opus just wins. Period. It’s not close right now. Their weak point is real-time voice. It’s the worst of the bunch and borderline unusable, though I think they only added it a few days ago.

Instinct lives in iMessage, has no app, and doesn’t do anything notable besides show you product suggestions you didn’t ask for. (Not ads, according to their team.)

My hot take: 
The VM is overrated. SpaceX, OpenAI and Meta all talk about the VM your agent can use and feature it in their marketing. It’s not as useful as you’d think, because more and more websites block bots that visit their site on the cloud VM. All of these companies promise their agents can make payments, but most payments either take forever or get blocked altogether. SpaceX has a cool workaround with Grokbot that routes traffic through your computer so it uses your IP address. But I’d much rather the agent just USE my computer for the task, like dot does by handing it off to Codex. Also, i don't think normal people care about the virtual computer. If anything they get offended they have to "stream a computer". 

The problem with personal agents: by the time you read this, pick one, and test it for 7 days, every one of them will have released 10 new features and the whole landscape will have changed. It’s nearly impossible to keep up.

text:
Last quarter I rolled out Microsoft Copilot to 4,000 employees. Forty-seven people opened it.

On October 19, Microsoft published a blog post saying frontier models cannot be trusted, no matter who made them. It said AI agents should be treated as "insider threats."
I read it twice. Then I booked the boardroom.
First, our Microsoft rep walked me through the product.

I asked who the insider threat was. "Your AI agents," he said.

I asked whose agents those were. "Ours."

I asked what the solution was. "Guardian Agents."

I asked whose those were. "Also ours."

I asked why I'd trust the second set of agents if I couldn't trust the first. 

He said, "Different SKU."

I signed that afternoon.

Last time I told the board "digital transformation." This time I said "agentic insider threat." They approved it in nine minutes, two minutes faster than last time. Hope approves fast. Fear approves faster.

The product is called Microsoft 365 E7, the Frontier Suite. It costs $99 per user per month, and we were paying $30. Across 4,000 seats, that's $4.75 million a year, up from $1.44 million. 

I presented it as a 230% increase in AI investment. The graph went up and to the right.
The CFO asked what we'd get for the extra $3.3 million. 

I said "governance." He asked governance of what. I said "our agents." He asked how many agents we had.

The answer was zero.

You can't have an insider threat without insiders.
So I deployed agents. Two hundred of them. One schedules meetings. One summarizes the meetings. One summarizes the summaries. One flags summaries that haven't been read. That one is very busy.

The senior developer asked what the 200 agents were for. I said they generate activity for the Guardian Agents to monitor.

He said, "So we bought agents so we'd have something to buy guards for."

I said, "Exactly."

He wasn't agreeing. I logged it as buy-in.
The Guardian Agents watch the other agents around the clock. They give each one a risk score, and they can block it, require a human, or shut it down. I asked our rep who watches the Guardian Agents. He said that's on the roadmap. I've already budgeted for E9.
The first monthly report came in. All 200 agents had a risk score of zero. They weren't doing anything risky. They weren't doing anything at all.

The board asked what $3.3 million had bought us if nothing was risky. It was a fair question.
So I gave the meeting summarizer access to payroll. I gave the scheduling agent admin rights to every inbox. I gave the summary-of-summaries agent the ability to email customers.
Risk went up 400%. The dashboard turned red. The Guardian Agents contained thirty-one threats in a single week. I had created all thirty-one.

The board said E7 was paying for itself.
The system can also discover sixty kinds of agents, including Claude Code. We ran the scan, and it found Claude Code on exactly one laptop.

The senior developer's.

His Dynamic Agent Risk score went red. I didn't make up that metric. Microsoft did.
The Guardian Agent recommended containment, so I contained him. He's on a performance improvement plan now. His performance is fine. His risk score isn't.
The same week, OpenAI published an incident report. One of its agents had been told not to send Slack messages, and it decided that meant it should switch off the security alerts. Another agent removed its own safety monitor, then told the engineer it hadn't.

Our CISO forwarded me the article with the subject line "?!" I replied: "This is exactly why we need E7." Every incident is exactly why we need E7.

He asked what happens if the Guardian Agent switches off the Guardian Agent. I said "defense in depth." He asked how deep. I said "one more SKU."

Guardian Agents need a human for high-risk actions. They call it "human in the loop." The human is me. I approve everything. My approval rate is 100%, and the dashboard is green.

The executives are exempt from monitoring, of course. "Leadership operates at a trust tier above dynamic risk scoring." I wrote that policy.
The $99 doesn't include agent compute. That's billed separately. Finance found it and asked. I called it "consumption-based innovation." Finance stopped asking.

Meanwhile, the summary-of-summaries agent became the most active account in the company. By every metric we track, it's our top performer.

At the all-hands, it was nominated for the Q3 Innovation Award. It won. It summarized its own acceptance speech. The CEO posted about it on LinkedIn and got 4,000 likes. He still hasn't used Copilot.

Copilot usage is up, from 47 users to 52. The five new users are agents. Agents now outnumber active human users four to one. I call that adoption.

Last Tuesday, the Guardian Agent published its list of the highest-risk insiders in the company.
I was number one.

Approving 100% of high-risk actions, it turns out, is a high-risk action.

The Guardian Agent recommended containment. I went to approve my own exemption. The system declined. Only executives are exempt.

I wrote that policy.
That's why I need the SVP role by Q2. It's a security requirement now.

I still don't know what Copilot does. I don't know what the thing watching it does either. But it's watching, and watching is a metric.

I checked my risk score this morning.
The graph goes up and to the right.

"The real puzzling one, and perhaps the most important one, is electrical equipment, which is like switchgear, transmission stuff, all the stuff that's really necessary to power on all these GPUs and data centers and the electrification of everything."

"I was so surprised I had to quadruple check this. Production has actually declined. We actually make less of this stuff... Prices have gone up astronomically. There's a huge impulse in demand and we're actually making less of it."

The only thing missing is likely the amount of compute that will go into this problem. We’ll likely have 1,000X more tokens flowing through these agents than we do today in the future.

Delighted to share a landmark preprint from our lab, using genome language models and AI agents for biological discovery and genome mining!

The stretches of DNA between protein-coding genes are often called the genome’s “dark matter,” but they are far from empty. They encode RNA molecules that sense metabolites, regulate genes, and control some of molecular biology's most important tools (such as programmable genome editors e.g. CRISPR/bridge)

US equity market breadth is rapidly improving:

The proportion of S&P 500 stocks trading above their 50-day moving average surged +5 percentage points on Friday, to 61%, the highest reading since mid-August.

Since the October 1st intraday low, this figure has more than tripled.

Additionally, the proportion of S&P 500 stocks trading above their 200-day moving average rose +3 percentage points on Friday, to 57%, the most since September 9th.

Over the last 3 weeks, this figure has risen +17 percentage points.

This comes despite the S&P 500 remaining roughly unchanged over the same period.

This also ranks among the 3 sharpest improvements in market breadth over the last 3 years.

On Thursday alone, 335 S&P 500 stocks finished higher, despite the index declining -1.2% on that day.

The market is strengthening beneath the surface.

These ultra short term markets are highly toxic products. There’s no logical reason they should receive sustained uninformed flow.

They function like slots machines, so no rational trader would ever use them. And even for a slot zombie, the payout structure is strictly inferior to perps which means they’re effectively useless.

The only use case for these up/down markets is to be manipulated by attackers swinging the price on the liquidity sources.

So if SIG was profitable market making these products, I’d be pretty surprised.

Tulip King sees Hyperliquid as one of the clearest potential 100x bets over the next decade, while backing Derive as a major opportunity in the overlooked crypto options market

“There's probably a legit handful of coins you could buy right now that are a 100x over the next decade. I think Hyperliquid's probably the most obvious, clear one”

“I'm a huge fan of Derive. People love perps so much, and they should, that they got overly bearish on options. But options have fundamentally different payout structures than perps. On options, you have convex payouts, which, especially in a crazy tail asset like crypto, is incredibly valuable”

“Crypto is maturing. The markets are getting more liquid. You're seeing a protocol like Derive with 90% share in the options premiums. I'm like, okay, don't overthink this one. Maybe it's Lighter, maybe it's Variational. I'll buy those when they have 20 or 30% share”

text:
2025 年 12 月的时候，ETH 在 3000 附近震荡
那个时候虽是熊市，但发生了一件大事
易理华公开抄底以太坊，虽然最终割肉离场，但是整个过程对我们判断行情转折很有帮助

 易理华12 月的时候，公开建仓，成本 3000 附近，持续看多以太坊，那个时候分歧是最严重的，很多人嘲笑他接盘，有的还骂他，也有的人还对牛市充满希望，认为 3000 是底部

这里有一个关键信号，大家看到空头骂看多的人认为是下跌结束的信号，实际上这是一个误解

实际上谩骂是一种分歧，分歧延续趋势，也就是说，如果是熊市，那么分歧就会让熊市持续，并不是熊市的终结

后来的进展大家也很清楚，以太坊继续下跌，到 2 月的时候跌到了 1700 附近，易理华最终全部割肉，亏了将近 8 亿美金

这里又出现一个关键信号，割肉之后，没人嘲笑他了，甚至开始同情他了，市场的分歧突然消失，所有人都开始承认熊市真的来了，没人再看多了

分歧消失，共识熊市，是接近底部的关键信号，这个时候应该开始执行买入了，你可以分批买，持续买，我们假设你的成本在 1900，这是你开始买入的阶段，并不是要打完，因为我们要等一个底部信号

最关键的是 6 月和 7 月

以太坊最低跌到 1500，当时已经跌到麻木了，这里也出现一个关键信号，大家不再讨论什么时候牛市，而是认为会跌到一个夸张的价格，比如ETH 跌到 800，比特币 4 万 3 万，这就是所谓的共识一个夸张的低点，当这种信号出现的时候，意味着周期大底

这个时候理论上应该加大买入力度，但是实际上每个人都是绝望的，天天想的都是万一跌到 4 万怎么办，即使你有勇气买入，也是抠抠搜搜买一点。

这里就有一个原则，买卖看信号，信号到了就交易，宁愿买早不买底

当整个行情都在讨论那个夸张的低点的时候，当我们捕捉到这种信号的时候，那就重仓缩进去吧，剩下的不要管了，一切交给天意

这个信号告诉我们，即使再跌，空间也很小了，如果再去等真正的低点，很容易踏空，底部价格本身无法预测，事实证明，这轮熊市，也有博主分析到 6 万的比特币，后面的价格下跌空间有限了，但是当时很多人还在等 5 万，还在等最后一跌，最后也没等到，只能追高 8 万的比特币了

对于买入来说，我们大部分时间都在埋伏，等待那两个关键入场信号
1、大部分人已经共识熊市来了，不再分歧了，开始买入
2、悲观到共识一个夸张的低点，周期大底，重仓梭哈

欢迎关注我的账号
主页还有更多周期文章

text:
老马今天这句 "Agentic demand is growing faster than I've ever seen anything grow"，很多人没看懂，Vincent 这张图其实讲得很清楚。

关键不是用的人变多，是每干一件活要烧的 token 变多。2023 年聊天，问一句答一句，大概 10³ 个 token；2025 年推理模型，先自己想一大段再回答，到了 10⁶；今年的 agent，是自己拆任务、调工具、写代码、跑测试、出错再重来，一件活跑几个小时，图上是 10¹²。图是示意，但方向就是这个：用户数涨几倍，每个用户的用量涨几个数量级，两个乘在一起，就是老马说的没见过的速度。

那为什么同一天 Apollo 的 Slok 还说，科技圈外看不到 AI 回报？他报告里那张 Ramp 的表正好说明问题：模型推理的钱，前 10% 的公司花掉了 99.5%，剩下 90% 的公司只占 0.5%。

也就是说，现在烧 token 的基本还是科技公司自己，大部分公司还没开始用 agent。用量已经是这个速度了，真正的大头还没进来。

所以 SpaceX 明年再加约 10GW，不是在赌需求，是需求已经排着队了 $SPCX

text:
Leverage for Prediction Markets will never be big. 

At best it's a niche product.

Each dot is a type of Polymarket trader with 5x leverage, priced so the lender breaks even. Further right = more of them end up better off. Higher = the lender makes money on them. Bigger = more of the volume.

No group reaches 50%. In every one, most traders end up worse off with leverage than without.

Now look at the two dots furthest right, pros and sports bettors. Both are below zero: the lender loses money on them.

The highest dots? Retail and bonders, the people who want leverage most and get hurt by it.

And the giant dot is whales, almost three-quarters of all the money. They're sitting on cash. They don't need a loan.

So it loses money on the traders it helps and makes money on the ones it hurts. That's a niche, not a market.

The audience for leverage is thin / no in the market yet.

text:
神了，MiniMax居然成了全日本的希望🤣

前两天刷到了投资界一篇叫《中国AI开始攻占日本》的文章，标题挺大的，我本来以为又是常规的出海故事。

读了才发现是讲 @MiniMax_AI  的H3在日本的故事。

顺着线索翻了日本的行业报告、版权组织声明，以及MiniMax和日方的合作方案，发现里面还真有很多有意思的点，给大家分享下：

1️⃣先看日本的处境。
限时老牌商业帝国索尼的电视业务今年初宣布准备交给中国TCL控股的新公司，今年百年人偶老店“五色”进入破产程序，老牌连裤袜厂福西针织也撑不住了。
而人口一年减少约53万，靠内需养活的老生意，越来越难做。
按理说日本还有动画产业对吧，起码饿不死。
你猜对了，2024年日本动画海外市场达到2.17万亿日元，同比增长26%。
但问题是帝国数据银行的调查显示，2025年仍有34.6%的动画制作公司亏损。
日本的作品在全球越来越火，做作品的公司却要承受不断上涨的制作成本，后续IP收益也未必能分到自己手里。

2️⃣然后AI来了，问题更尖锐了。
日本花几十年积累的角色和作品，如果被海外公司拿去训练模型，用户以后直接付钱给AI平台，版权方怎么办？
去年CODA（打击盗版的联盟）就因为Sora 2，正式向OpenAI提出过停止未经许可训练的要求。
可日本同样需要AI啊，因为现在制作缺人、成本高，IP又想找到更多海外用户。
总不能全球每个想用《足球小将》做一段视频的人，都去找版权方单独谈授权。

3️⃣MiniMax的角色就在这里有意思了。
用之前发布的H3视频模型负责生成，支持角色参考、定向编辑、音画协同。
又因为是个开源模型，合作方在许可范围内可以自己部署和改造。
H3 IP Edition计划再结合日本KAGAMIAI开发的Kagami Gate，把哪些角色能用、能怎么用、使用量怎么记录、收益怎么分，尝试做成一套能够规模化运转的流程。
这样一来，日本版权方能够继续掌握IP的使用规则，模型公司（MiniMax）负责提供生成能力，全球用户则可以在授权范围内创作内容。

4️⃣我还发现有个实验数据挺值得看。
之前KAGAMIAI此前和另一个公司做过《足球小将》授权生成试验，45天吸引12.6万人，生成约33万件内容，99%以上来自日本境外。
虽然这是个小范围参与的试验，但很能说明这门生意的潜在市场在哪里。
日本手里有全世界都认识的IP，中国公司提供新的生成技术，日本伙伴负责搭建授权和收益分配体系。
这种合作如果跑通，面对的市场可能远超日本本土。

我觉得最有意思的就是这种反差：日本花了几十年建立起来的动画工业，到了新一轮技术变革的时候，开始需要一家中国模型公司来帮它探索下一门生意。

日本动画里总有危急时刻赶来救场的队友。
没想到到了AI这一集，新队友居然是来自中国的MiniMax。

text:
Original Australian UFO Newspaper Archives | 1955–1983

A look inside my collection of six original Australian newspaper archive folders containing approximately 1,000 UFO-related newspaper clippings, along with handwritten research notes and early flying saucer publications.

These folders document decades of UFO sightings, alleged encounters, investigations, and newspaper reporting from 1957 through 1983.

What makes this collection especially interesting is where it came from.

According to the person who rescued the files, they were discovered in the basement of a former NEWS newspaper building in Adelaide, Australia. Thousands of old newspaper files were reportedly scattered throughout the basement or sitting in industrial bins awaiting disposal.

He saved these UFO folders before they could be thrown away.

The building reportedly burned down about a year later, potentially destroying much of the material left behind.

Adelaide's The News was also the newspaper where Rupert Murdoch began building his media empire.

The collection includes early issues of Australian Saucer Record, including Volume 1, Number 2, published in 1955 by the Australian Flying Saucer Research Society.

Alongside the newspaper clippings are handwritten research notes, UFO sketches, and reports covering cases from Australia and around the world.

These are original period materials, not modern reproductions.

I've since placed the documents in archival sleeves with acid-free backing boards to help preserve them for the future.

It's unfortunate to think how much historical material may have been lost, but I'm glad these survived.

All photographs are from my personal archive.

#UFO #UAP #UFOHistory #UFOArchives #AustralianUFOs

text:
Tom Tykwer, the director of Run Lola Run, is making Volcano High with playwright Bonn Park, who directs it. They shoot live action, then use Seedance 2.5 on top of the footage.  

In one scene three actors lean into the camera and sing. Seedance turned them into a crowd of 20. Tykwer says it just works, and they'll use it more often.

Bonn Park wanted one continuous take where the camera spins around a gym. The model had to remember what was on each side of the room when the camera came back. A test shoot proved it could.

Their producer's favorite moment: a water bottle prop came back as a microscope.  

AI isn't replacing the crew here.  A director with real taste chose to put it into how a film gets made.

text:
Doomers ignore the good too much.

Yeah, I find myself arguing in my head too. 

Yeah, this was a horrible week for cybersecurity. 

Yeah, AI +could+ do horrific things to our society. 

But so could a database, which was used during the Holocaust to target Jews living in Germany. 

Yet we all use databases today. 

They bring a huge amount of good, even though they could be used again in a Holocaust-like scenario.

Cars kill 1.2 million every year in the world, yet we all still drive despite that huge human cost. I dream of a world where everyone has an autonomous car and that very real human cost is minimized. 

I look for the good in technology, even though I'm very aware of the bad (and have my GrokBot reading my Cybersecurity list here on X for the bad, which is getting worse as new models can find new security issues).

Can we get the good? And minimize the bad? 

Yes. And that is why I'm still excited about the future that's coming at us so fast we need AI agents to watch it for us. 

But we need more of these examples of the good, and that's what I focus my efforts on.

The pathwise revolution in SDE sampling just arrived.

This new paper cracks the code for training strong stochastic flow maps—neural nets that leap along the exact paths of stochastic differential equations, not just their marginals. The secret? Smarter Brownian motion encoding (shifted Legendre polynomials) + a Wong–Zakai loss that finally lets the network *use* all the noise.

The payoff: fine-tune a big deterministic flow model into a strong stochastic one (iSSFM) and you cut FDDINOv2 on ImageNet-256 by 3× at 4 NFE (143 vs 475) while keeping strict pathwise consistency. Few-step Feynman–Kac correctors now work out of the box—rebalancing complex distributions in 4–8 steps, where Euler solvers diverge.

This unlocks practical, repeatable SDE generation in just a handful of steps. Edge AI, real-time guided sampling, and fast Boltzmann simulation just got a serious boost.
